title: The Hangover
logline: Three friends retrace a lost night in Las Vegas to find the groom. Situational and shock comedy.
overview: When three friends finally come to after a raucous night of bachelor-party revelry, they find a baby in the closet and a tiger in the bathroom. But they can't seem to locate their best friend, Doug – who's supposed to be tying the knot. Launching a frantic search for Doug, the trio perseveres through a nasty hangover to try to make it to the church on time.
tagline: Some guys just can't handle Vegas.

jokes.text: Hey, this is Phil. Leave me a message, or don't. Do me a favor. Don't text me, it's gay.
jokes.setup: We're hearing a series of mundane voicemail greetings for Doug, Stu, and then Phil.
jokes.punchline: Phil's voicemail is aggressively casual and ends with the absurdly casual homophobic non-sequitur 'Don't text me, it's gay,' establishing him immediately as an irreverent, selfish character.
jokes.explanation: Works beautifully as character introduction — after two normal voicemails, Phil's shows contempt for social norms and basic courtesy. The '...or don't' is a perfect economy beat. The final line is edgy but functions as pure character establishment. High character integration because only someone like Phil would have this voicemail.

jokes.text: He's probably on a heater. And you never walk away from the table when you're on a heater.
jokes.setup: Tracy is panicking that the groom is missing the morning of his wedding. Sid is trying to offer reassurance.
jokes.punchline: Sid's 'reassurance' is that Doug is probably gambling and you never leave a hot streak — delivered with sincere conviction, completely tone-deaf to the wedding context.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Sid prioritizes gambling logic over his daughter's wedding anxiety. The punchline lands because his reasoning is internally consistent but socially absurd. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: You do if you're getting married.
jokes.setup: Sid just said 'You never walk away from the table when you're on a heater.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy's flat, devastating comeback punctures his gambling logic with the obvious reality.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that do real work. The deadpan delivery implied in the line undercuts Sid's confident gambling logic. Gets a solid chuckle but isn't exceptional material.

jokes.text: Yeah. That's not gonna happen.
jokes.setup: Tracy says 'We're getting married in 5 hours.' Phil pauses, then responds.
jokes.punchline: The blunt, unhelpful confirmation from Phil — delivered with apparent calm — that the wedding is simply not happening. The beat before it makes it land harder.
jokes.explanation: Phil's total emotional detachment from Tracy's crisis is perfectly in character. The pause implied before the line, plus its bluntness, make this a strong character beat. Economy is excellent — it's funny precisely because it offers nothing useful.

jokes.text: Whoa, watch it pervert! / It's okay Alan, he's just doing your inseam. / It's getting very close to my shaft.
jokes.setup: Alan is being measured by a tailor. He reacts with alarm.
jokes.punchline: Alan's visceral paranoia about the tailor's proximity to his groin — 'it's getting very close to my shaft' — immediately establishes his social dysfunction and inappropriate candor.
jokes.explanation: Effective Alan introduction — 'shaft' is an unexpected word choice that reveals his oblivious directness. The escalation from 'pervert' to the clinical 'shaft' is good. Character integration is high because this response only comes from someone with Alan's particular social wiring.

jokes.text: I want you to know, Doug, I'm a steel-trap. Whatever happens tonight, I will never, ever, speak a word of it.
jokes.setup: Alan wants to reassure Doug that bringing him along won't be a problem.
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'steel-trap' paired with Alan's demonstrated social dysfunction makes the promise absurdly unconvincing. It's a boast that lands as a threat.
jokes.explanation: Solid character-building joke. Alan's sincerity makes it funnier — he genuinely believes he's being reassuring. Works best in context of what we've already seen from him.

jokes.text: I don't care what happens. I don't care if we kill someone.
jokes.setup: Alan is trying to assure Doug he can handle anything. He escalates his examples of discretion.
jokes.punchline: The leap from 'whatever happens' platitudes to casually mentioning murder as an example of a keepable secret is a massive tonal jump that gets a big laugh.
jokes.explanation: One of the first great Alan jokes. The escalation from reassurance to 'I don't care if we kill someone' is perfectly executed — no windup, completely sincere. It works because Alan isn't being edgy; he genuinely thinks this is a helpful thing to say. High character integration and strong economy.

jokes.text: And Phil either. I don't like him.
jokes.setup: Sid is listing conditions for lending his car — don't let Alan drive, don't let Phil drive.
jokes.punchline: The reason given for Phil not driving isn't safety concerns — it's purely personal: 'I don't like him.' Blunt, honest, and funnier for being so simple.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. After the legitimate safety concern about Alan, the pivot to pure dislike for Phil is unexpected and honest. Sid is established as someone who says exactly what he thinks with no filter.

jokes.text: Except for Herpes. That shit'll come back with you.
jokes.setup: Sid sends the guys off with the classic Vegas sign-off: 'What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately adds the medical exception — herpes doesn't stay in Vegas. Delivered with complete sincerity and authority.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. It takes a deeply familiar cultural cliché and subverts it with a specific, medically accurate exception delivered with total confidence. The word 'shit'll' gives it a blue-collar authority. Highly quotable, strong structure, and genuinely clever twist on an overused phrase. Earns its high impact score.

jokes.text: Pay now or forever regret missing out on this experience of a lifetime, guys.
jokes.setup: Phil is collecting permission slips and money from his students for a field trip — framed exactly like a cool salesman pitch.
jokes.punchline: He's using the language of a Vegas hype pitch to collect $90 from elementary school children for a trip to a science observatory. The mismatch is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Effective character establishment — Phil treats his students the way a con artist treats marks. 'Experience of a lifetime' for the Griffith Observatory is a great contrast. Works mainly as character comedy showing Phil's contempt for his job and the people around him.

jokes.text: I'm not supposed to be within 200 feet of a school. / Or Chuck E. Cheese.
jokes.setup: Phil parks outside the school. Alan notes discomfort about being near the school.
jokes.punchline: He's not worried about the car or social awkwardness — he has a legal restraining order that covers schools AND Chuck E. Cheese, which he mentions as a casual afterthought.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The two-beat structure is perfect: the 200-foot restraining order is already a huge character revelation, but adding 'Or Chuck E. Cheese' as a beat-later afterthought is what makes it exceptional. The Chuck E. Cheese addition implies a separate, specific incident. The pause between lines is essential and implies Alan genuinely didn't think the second part was important enough to lead with. High originality, near-perfect structure, and extremely high character integration — this could only be Alan.

jokes.text: It's the weekend, Nick. I don't know you. You do not exist.
jokes.setup: A student enthusiastically greets Phil outside the school.
jokes.punchline: Phil dismisses his student's existence entirely in precise, escalating terms — 'I don't know you. You do not exist.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phil characterization. The escalation from 'it's the weekend' to full ontological denial ('you do not exist') is perfectly constructed. It's not just 'I'm off duty' — it's the existential erasure of a child that reveals Phil's character efficiently. High character integration.

jokes.text: Don't forget your Rogaine. / Rogaine, check. / And don't forget to use it. I can totally tell when you forget. Your hair just looks thinner.
jokes.setup: Stu says a seemingly routine goodbye to his girlfriend Melissa.
jokes.punchline: Melissa is packing in a reminder about Stu's Rogaine, then doubles down with a targeted insult about his hair looking thinner when he forgets. It's controlling and cruel while being framed as caring.
jokes.explanation: Effective cringe comedy establishing Melissa as controlling and subtly cruel. 'I can totally tell when you forget' is the key beat — she's monitoring him. The audience's discomfort at Stu's docile 'Using of the Rogaine, check' laugh is the real payoff. Good character establishment.

jokes.text: Melissa, we're going to Napa Valley. I don't even think they have strip clubs in wine country.
jokes.setup: Melissa accuses Stu of going to strip clubs. Stu lies about their destination (they're going to Vegas).
jokes.punchline: Stu is already lying about where they're going, making his denial of strip clubs doubly absurd since they're headed to Las Vegas — the strip club capital of the world.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony — audience knows they're going to Vegas — does most of the work. Stu's particular confidence ('I don't even think they have strip clubs in wine country') while lying about the destination is a nice character beat. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: And the worst part is that little girl grinding, and dry humping the fucking stage up there. That's somebody's daughter up there. / That's somebody's daughter up there. / I was just gonna say that.
jokes.setup: Melissa is ranting about how gross strip clubs are. Stu is agreeing enthusiastically.
jokes.punchline: Stu is so trained in agreeing with Melissa that he accidentally steals her punchline mid-delivery, then claims he was 'just gonna say that' — revealing total psychological subjugation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe beat. The fact that Stu finishes Melissa's sentence — having apparently internalized her complete worldview — and then claims credit is a devastating character detail. It says everything about their relationship dynamic without being explicit. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Paging Doctor Faggot. Doctor Faggot.
jokes.setup: Stu is in the middle of an earnest, submissive goodbye to Melissa. Phil intercuts with a hospital PA-style announcement.
jokes.punchline: Phil pages 'Doctor Faggot' over what appears to be a hospital intercom (or is shouting from outside) precisely to humiliate Stu mid-goodbye and signal contempt for his relationship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Crude but effective. The joke works on two levels: the interruption of the cringe sequence, and Phil's specific contempt for Stu's emasculated state. The 'Doctor' prefix makes it land — Phil knows Stu takes pride in his title. Earns its laugh through timing and delivery rather than sophisticated writing.

jokes.text: That's a good idea, Dr. Faggot.
jokes.setup: Stu says 'I should go' after the paging incident.
jokes.punchline: Melissa echoes the insult back to Stu without irony — she agrees with Phil's assessment, using the slur as a send-off.
jokes.explanation: The callback landing from Melissa is the real joke here — she adopts Phil's nickname, which both deepens her cruelty and reveals she thinks Phil is right. It's a perfect character moment that arrives as a callback punchline. Good economy.

jokes.text: Road trip! / Hey, Vegas! Vegas, baby. / Vegas.
jokes.setup: The three guys finally escape and get in the car.
jokes.punchline: Phil and Doug go full hype mode ('Road trip! Vegas baby!') and Alan's contribution is a single flat 'Vegas.' — the same word, completely deflated.
jokes.explanation: Alan's flat one-word 'Vegas.' is a subtle but effective character beat. After Phil and Doug's enthusiasm, Alan's match in content but complete deflation in energy is both funny and revealing. Relies on Alan's socially off delivery.

jokes.text: What, are you a cop now? You know I drive great when I'm drunk. / That's true. Don't forget Phil was always our designated drunk driver.
jokes.setup: Phil is drinking while asking to drive. Stu refuses. Phil deflects.
jokes.punchline: Doug casually confirms that Phil's designated role in their friend group was 'drunk driver' — said as a nostalgic fond memory.
jokes.explanation: The 'designated drunk driver' as a nostalgic institution is a great dark joke. Doug's matter-of-fact delivery ('don't forget...') implies this was a known and accepted arrangement. Good character comedy — it confirms Phil's recklessness while also showing Doug's laid-back complicity.

jokes.text: Guys, my dad loves this car more than he loves me, so yeah.
jokes.setup: Phil is pushing to drive. Doug explains why the car can't be driven by Phil.
jokes.punchline: Doug's explanation reveals a dark family dynamic — his dad literally prioritizes the car over him — delivered as a casual, matter-of-fact statement.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — the dark self-deprecation lands because Doug says it without self-pity. The 'so yeah' at the end is a perfect button. Slight because it's one of many quick jokes in this sequence.

jokes.text: I left my wife and my kid at home so I can go with you guys to Vegas. Do you know how difficult that was? / It's really sweet, Phil. / I was being sarcastic. I fucking hate my life. I may never go back. I might just stay in Vegas.
jokes.setup: Phil mentions sacrificing time with family to attend the bachelor party — which initially sounds touching.
jokes.punchline: Phil immediately clarifies he was being sarcastic and that he hates his life, seriously entertaining the idea of abandoning his family in Vegas.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Phil jokes in the reel. The misdirect — letting Doug respond warmly before Phil's brutal correction — is structurally solid. 'I fucking hate my life' delivered with sincerity is funny precisely because Phil has no self-pity filter. 'I may never go back' as a genuine option is dark and in character. High character integration.

jokes.text: You know, Doug, you should enjoy yourself, because come Saturday you're gonna start dying a little bit. Every day.
jokes.setup: Phil is lamenting his own married life, then pivots to deliver unsolicited advice to the groom-to-be.
jokes.punchline: The grim prediction — marriage as a gradual, daily death — is delivered with the authority of lived experience.
jokes.explanation: Classic married-man-at-bachelor-party material, elevated slightly by Phil's specific cadence and the 'every day' as a separate clause. Not highly original but delivered with commitment. The setup context (Phil just said he hates his life) makes it land better than it would in isolation.

jokes.text: That's why I managed to stay single this whole time. / Oh, really? That's why you're single? / Yeah. / Cool. Good to know.
jokes.setup: Phil delivers a speech about marriage killing you slowly. Alan takes it as a personal win.
jokes.punchline: Alan presents his singleness as a deliberate life strategy — implying he chose it. Phil's response ('Oh, really? That's why you're single?') drips with the implication that Alan is single for very different, unspoken reasons.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed exchange. Alan's earnest pride in his 'choice' to be single, Phil's withering response, and Alan's completely unbothered 'Yeah' creates a layered comedic moment. Phil's 'Cool. Good to know.' is a perfect button — total dismissal after the revelation. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: Oh, Jesus Christ! / Oh, my God. / That was awesome. / That was not awesome! What's wrong with you. / That was insane. We almost just die. / You should've seen your face. It's classic.
jokes.setup: While driving on the highway, something happens (inferred: Alan does something dangerous, possibly sticking his hand/body out the window, or a near-miss).
jokes.punchline: Alan's total lack of fear and delight ('That was awesome') while Stu panics, combined with 'You should've seen your face. It's classic' — Alan enjoying Stu's terror is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Likely a visual gag that the transcript diminishes — Alan doing something dangerous on the highway would play much bigger on screen. The dialogue aftermath is functional but the real laugh comes from what we can't see. Moderate score given transcript-only view.

jokes.text: Don't touch it. / Don't even look at it. Go on. Get out. You heard me. / Don't look at me either. / Yeah, you better walk on.
jokes.setup: They stop at a gas station. A stranger compliments or approaches Sid's car.
jokes.punchline: Alan's escalating territorial hostility toward the stranger — from 'don't touch it' to 'don't look at it' to 'don't look at ME either' — is delightfully unhinged self-appointed guardianship.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. Alan extends his protection from the car to himself ('Don't look at me either') which is a perfect absurdist leap. The 'Yeah, you better walk on' is Alan talking tough to someone who has already left, showing complete lack of social calibration. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: He's actually kind of funny. / Yeah, he means well. / I'll hit an old man in public.
jokes.setup: Phil and Doug are watching Alan's gas station antics from a distance and mildly defending him.
jokes.punchline: Alan overhears (or simply continues), and declares — apparently without context — that he would hit an old man in public. It's delivered as a credential or a warning.
jokes.explanation: One of the most economical Alan jokes in the reel. Five words that establish Alan's threat assessment, complete lack of social boundaries, and total sincerity. The randomness of 'old man specifically' is perfect — why an old man? Alan has clearly thought about this. Very high character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Jesus, he's like a gremlin. Comes with instructions and shit.
jokes.setup: Phil and Doug are discussing Alan's care instructions from Tracy — no gambling, not too much drinking.
jokes.punchline: Phil summarizes Alan as a gremlin — a creature that comes with dangerous rules you must follow or face chaos.
jokes.explanation: Good metaphor — gremlins are pop culture shorthand for 'harmless until certain conditions are violated, then dangerous.' Applied to Alan it's specific and apt. 'Comes with instructions and shit' is a good button. Quotable.

jokes.text: So you can't go to Vegas but she can fuck a bellhop on a carnival cruise line.
jokes.setup: Phil is pointing out the double standard in Stu's relationship — Stu has to lie about going to Vegas, yet Melissa has apparently cheated.
jokes.punchline: Phil drops the cruise ship infidelity as a trump card, with the specific details ('bellhop,' 'carnival cruise line') adding comic texture and implying he's rehearsed this argument.
jokes.explanation: Phil's specificity makes this — he doesn't just say 'she cheated,' he has a fully detailed account with venue and profession. The escalation from Stu's one lie to Melissa's infidelity is effective. Good character moment for Phil as the friend who keeps score.

jokes.text: Okay, first of all, he was a bartender. And she was wasted. / And you believe that? / Yeah I do believe that. Because she's grossed out by semen.
jokes.setup: Stu tries to defend Melissa against Phil's accusation, correcting the job title and offering context.
jokes.punchline: Stu's final defense — that Melissa couldn't have fully cheated because 'she's grossed out by semen' — is a staggering overshare that reveals both his delusion and his TMI candor.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe escalation. The sequence moves from 'he was a bartender not a bellhop' (ridiculous defense) to 'she was wasted' (worse defense) to 'she's grossed out by semen' as the clincher. Each beat is worse than the last. The final line is the standout — Stu offers private physiological information as exculpatory evidence with zero awareness of how it sounds. High character integration.

jokes.text: That'll be $32.50.
jokes.setup: Stu has just said 'Because she's grossed out by semen' at full volume in what turns out to be a convenience store with a cashier present.
jokes.punchline: The cashier's completely flat 'That'll be $32.50' — no acknowledgment, no reaction — after Stu's intimate revelation is a perfect deadpan context joke.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic timing joke. The audience has been absorbed in the conversation and forgotten they're in public — the cashier's line snaps everyone back to social reality. The complete non-reaction is funnier than any reaction would have been. Maximum economy (four words). The setup is entirely earned by the preceding dialogue.

jokes.text: It says here we should work in teams. Who wants to be my spotter?
jokes.setup: Alan is apparently reading a card-counting manual.
jokes.punchline: Alan has prepared for Vegas with an instruction manual on card counting and is treating it like a team sport requiring a 'spotter,' with professional seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Good Alan joke — his over-preparation and treating a casino as a military operation is in character. The 'spotter' request implies he has absorbed the full methodology from a book but doesn't understand the social context. Character integration is strong.

jokes.text: It's not illegal. It's frowned upon. Like masturbating on an airplane.
jokes.setup: Stu says card counting is illegal. Alan disputes this, reaching for an analogy.
jokes.punchline: The analogy Alan chooses to illustrate something 'frowned upon but not illegal' is masturbating on an airplane — delivered with complete confidence as a reasonable comparison.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire reel and one of the strongest Alan jokes in the film. The structure is perfect: legal status is the topic, an analogy is promised, and then the specific analogy chosen is airplane masturbation — a very particular act that Alan treats as universally understood shorthand for 'frowned upon but technically okay.' The implication that Alan has thought this through — or has personal experience — is what gives it its depth. Near-perfect character integration, originality, structure, and economy. Highly quotable, big room laugh.

jokes.text: I'm pretty sure that's illegal too. / Yeah, maybe after 9/11 where everybody gets so sensitive.
jokes.setup: Stu points out that masturbating on an airplane is also illegal.
jokes.punchline: Alan blames post-9/11 security sensitivity for the prohibition on airplane masturbation — implying it was fine before — and expresses exasperation at the overreaction.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback and escalation. The joke on its own (blaming 9/11 for airplane masturbation restrictions) would be strong, but as a continuation of Alan's previous logic, it's brilliant. Alan isn't being edgy — he genuinely believes this historical/policy narrative. The '9/11 where everybody gets so sensitive' as an explanation is a masterpiece of character-specific absurdist logic. Very high all around.

jokes.text: Thanks a lot, Bin Laden.
jokes.setup: Alan has just blamed 9/11 for airplane masturbation laws.
jokes.punchline: Alan directly addresses (blames) Bin Laden for his personal inconvenience — as though airplane masturbation restrictions are a primary legacy of the 9/11 attacks.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the airplane masturbation sequence. Three words that serve as a direct address to a historical figure, holding him personally accountable for what Alan considers a profound injustice. The economy is extraordinary. The character integration is perfect — only Alan's particular brain connects these dots and then speaks them aloud. One of the most quotable lines in the reel.

jokes.text: Maybe we should tell that to Rain Man, because he practically bankrupted the casino and he was a 'ratard.' / He was a 'ratard.' / Retard.
jokes.setup: Stu says you have to be super smart to count cards. Alan disputes this by citing Rain Man.
jokes.punchline: Alan mispronounces 'retard' as 'ratard' — not as an insult but as what he genuinely believes the word is — and Stu has to correct him, which Alan confirms with his own (still wrong) repetition.
jokes.explanation: Alan's mispronunciation reveals genuine ignorance rather than malice — he's not being dismissive, he literally doesn't know the word. Stu's correction followed by Alan's repetition of the same wrong word is a great structural beat. High character integration — Alan is the only character in the group who could genuinely not know this. The Rain Man argument itself is also a solid absurdist logic point.

jokes.text: Dr. Price? Stu, you're a dentist. And don't try and get fancy.
jokes.setup: Stu checks in at Caesar's under 'Dr. Price.' Phil reacts.
jokes.punchline: Phil's dismissal of Stu's professional title — 'you're a dentist' — delivered as a deflation, plus 'don't try and get fancy' implies Stu routinely overreaches with his title.
jokes.explanation: Solid running character beat — Phil's contempt for Stu's professional pretension is a consistent throughline. 'Don't try and get fancy' implies this is a known habit. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: And if someone has a heart attack, you should still call 911.
jokes.setup: Phil is continuing to diminish Stu's medical credentials in front of the hotel check-in clerk.
jokes.punchline: Phil instructs the hotel staff that Stu's being a 'doctor' should not be relied upon in an emergency — delivered to the clerk as genuine consumer advice.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the dentist joke. Phil addressing the clerk directly with this warning is a nice absurdist touch — he's concerned enough about false advertising to intervene on behalf of strangers. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Can I ask you a question? Do you know if the hotel is pager-friendly? I'm not getting a sig' on my beeper. / Is there a payphone bank? Bunch of payphones? Business. / There's a phone in your room. / That'll work.
jokes.setup: They're checking into a luxury hotel in 2009. Alan has concerns about communication technology.
jokes.punchline: Alan is concerned about his pager signal and looking for payphones — technology that was obsolete a decade prior. His final acceptance of a room phone ('That'll work') is delivered with relief.
jokes.explanation: Alan's anachronistic tech concerns are a great character detail — it places him outside of normal time. The specific 'sig on my beeper' and the 'bunch of payphones? Business.' query are both strong. 'That'll work' as a satisfied resolution to his problem is a perfect button. High character integration.

jokes.text: You probably get this a lot. This isn't the real Caesar's Palace, is it? / What do you mean? / Did Caesar live here? / No. / I didn't think so.
jokes.setup: Alan approaches the check-in clerk with what he frames as a knowing, worldly question.
jokes.punchline: Alan genuinely believes Julius Caesar may have lived at Caesar's Palace and has apparently been debating this internally. His 'I didn't think so' implies he suspected but needed confirmation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Alan moments in the reel. 'You probably get this a lot' establishes Alan thinks he's asking a sophisticated question. 'Did Caesar live here?' is the reveal of his actual mental model. 'I didn't think so' — delivered as though he's confirmed a suspicion — is the perfect button. The gap between Alan's self-perception and his actual question is the core of his character, executed perfectly here.

jokes.text: I just wish you could see this place, because you, of all people, would love it. Yeah. No, it's so quiet. There's no TVs, no phones. They just have this cute little antique radios in all the rooms.
jokes.setup: Stu is on the phone with Melissa, describing their villa — but he's lying about being in Napa, so he has to describe it in terms that fit a wine country inn.
jokes.punchline: Stu is describing a massive Vegas villa — presumably loaded with TVs and entertainment — as a quaint, quiet Napa retreat with 'antique radios,' spinning every luxury into rustic charm for Melissa's benefit.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained irony joke — the audience knows they're in Vegas, so every detail Stu offers is doubly funny. 'Antique radios in all the rooms' is a great specific lie. The 'of all people, you would love it' aimed at Melissa is a nice touch since she hates Vegas.

jokes.text: Caesar Palace. Yeah, like the salad.
jokes.setup: Stu is on the phone with Melissa describing the villa. She apparently asks who runs the place.
jokes.punchline: In his haste to maintain the Napa cover story, Stu invents a proprietor named 'Caesar Palace' and then clarifies 'like the salad' — accidentally making his lie even more absurd.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. 'Caesar Palace — like the salad' is a perfect improvised lie that creates its own absurdity. The 'like the salad' clarification is unnecessary and makes it worse, which is exactly why it's funny. It also retroactively makes Alan's earlier Caesar question (joke 39) land harder as a thematic echo.

jokes.text: What the hell is that? / What do you think it is? / That's what I think it is. I think it's a big fucking mistake.
jokes.setup: Stu has something to show Doug and Phil — something he's kept secret. The anticipation is established.
jokes.punchline: It's a diamond ring. Phil's response — 'I think it's a big fucking mistake' — is a straight read of the situation (he's going to propose to a woman who cheated on him) delivered as an aesthetic opinion.
jokes.explanation: Good Phil joke. His interpretation of 'big fucking mistake' works on two levels: literally (the ring IS a mistake given their relationship) and as blunt editorial. The beat before he says it — 'That's what I think it is' — is nicely constructed.

jokes.text: What the hell is that? / What do you think it is? / That's what I think it is. I think it's a big fucking mistake.
jokes.setup: Stu reveals something — context indicates it's an engagement ring — that he's planning to use to propose to Melissa at Doug's wedding.
jokes.punchline: Phil's response to seeing the ring: 'I think it's a big fucking mistake.' Not even a beat — immediate and total condemnation.
jokes.explanation: Phil's response is perfectly in character — he has no filter and genuinely believes Melissa is awful. The mirror structure ('What do you think it is?' / 'That's what I think it is') is a nice construction before the punchline.

jokes.text: A, that is bullshit. And B, she is a complete bitch. / Hey, that's his fiancée. / It's true. You know it's true. She beats him. / That was twice and I was out of line. She's strong-willed. And I respect that.
jokes.setup: Phil calls Melissa a bitch. Doug mildly objects. Phil escalates to 'she beats him.'
jokes.punchline: Stu's defense — 'That was twice and I was out of line. She's strong-willed. And I respect that.' — is a devastating cringe revelation that confirms the abuse while framing it as a character virtue he admires.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Stu jokes in the film. The structure is perfect: Phil's accusation seems like exaggeration, Doug gently pushes back, then Stu's 'That was twice' confirms it. But it's 'She's strong-willed. And I respect that.' that elevates it from shocking to brilliant — Stu has not only rationalized being hit but reframed the abuser's trait as admirable. It's dark, specific, and entirely Stu. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: A, that is bullshit. And B, she is a complete bitch.
jokes.setup: Stu explains he and Melissa have been together three years so it's 'time' — following 'the rules.'
jokes.punchline: Phil's formal enumeration ('A... and B...') applied to what is essentially a primal emotional rejection is funny. The clinical structure undercuts the content.
jokes.explanation: Solid Phil moment. The 'A... and B...' formalism is very Phil — applying structure to contempt. Good economy, character-consistent.

jokes.text: Not to mention she fucked the sailor. / He wasn't a sailor. He was a bartender on a cruise ship. You know that.
jokes.setup: Phil is cataloguing Melissa's offenses. Stu reflexively corrects the professional title.
jokes.punchline: Even in the context of defending against a cheating accusation, Stu's priority is correcting 'sailor' to 'bartender on a cruise ship' — the precision reveals how thoroughly he has processed and compartmentalized this.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the earlier gas station conversation — Phil has upgraded the cheating guy from 'bellhop' to 'sailor,' and Stu again corrects him with the specific title, showing both Stu's compulsive precision and how often this topic has apparently been discussed.

jokes.text: Guys, I'm standing right here, so I can hear everything you're saying.
jokes.setup: Phil and Doug have been discussing Stu's relationship as though he's not present — a sustained beat of talking around him.
jokes.punchline: Stu's reminder that he's physically present and auditorally functional, delivered as a sincere heads-up rather than an outburst.
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. The joke is in the gentleness of the reminder — Stu isn't angry, just informing them. It's a standard comedic beat but Stu's specific defeated delivery makes it work in context.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, you ready to let the dogs out? / What? / Let the dogs out. You know, like, who let the dogs out. / Who brought this guy along?
jokes.setup: The heavy emotional conversation ends. Alan bursts in with energy to get the night started.
jokes.punchline: Alan's hype phrase is 'let the dogs out' — referencing the 2000 Baha Men song — with zero awareness that this is chronologically and culturally dated. Phil's 'Who brought this guy along?' reacts to Alan's obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Good Alan moment — his enthusiasm is genuine but his cultural reference is absurd. Phil's response ('Who brought this guy along?') is funny given that Phil knows exactly who brought him (Doug, who is standing right there). Character integration high for Alan.

jokes.text: You're not really wearing that, are you? / Wearing what? / The man purse. / You're actually gonna wear that or you guys just fuckin' with me? / This is where I keep all my things. I get a lot of compliments on this. / Plus it's not a man purse. It's called a satchel. Indiana Jones wears one. / So does Joy Behar.
jokes.setup: Alan emerges from his room wearing a satchel/man-purse. Phil and Stu react.
jokes.punchline: Alan defends his satchel by citing Indiana Jones as a cultural precedent. Stu immediately counters with Joy Behar — a morning talk show host — as a comparable example, undercutting Alan's masculine frame.
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup-punchline with great structure. Alan's escalating defense — 'I get compliments,' 'it's a satchel,' 'Indiana Jones wears one' — builds perfectly toward Stu's Joy Behar counter. The specificity of Joy Behar (not a generic female celebrity) makes it land harder. Alan's obliviousness to his own defenses undercutting him is core character work. Very quotable — 'it's not a man purse, it's a satchel' has become a cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: I'm just saying it's clearly marked, okay? We're definitely not supposed to be up here. / C'mon, Stu. We're paying for the villa. We can do whatever the fuck we want.
jokes.setup: The group has accessed what appears to be a restricted area of the hotel (the roof).
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'we're paying for the villa, we can do whatever the fuck we want' as a legal/moral framework for ignoring clearly posted restrictions is a perfect expression of his character.
jokes.explanation: Solid Phil/Stu dynamic joke. Phil's reasoning — that money grants unlimited license — is entirely in character. Stu's anxiety vs. Phil's entitlement is a reliable comedic pairing.

jokes.text: A little Jägermeister. Good idea. / Good call. / On the roof.
jokes.setup: Alan has produced a bottle of Jägermeister from his satchel on the roof of Caesar's Palace.
jokes.punchline: The approvals are delivered as if Alan has made a sensible logistical choice. 'On the roof' as the final endorsement — the location itself making the drink seem better — is a good dry button.
jokes.explanation: Mild beat. The satchel paying off as a Jägermeister delivery system is a small callback to the bag joke. 'On the roof' is a decent dry button but the joke is thin. Functional.

jokes.text: To Doug and Tracy. May tonight be but a minor speed-bump in an otherwise very long and healthy marriage.
jokes.setup: Phil is asked to give a toast on the roof of Caesar's Palace. He raises his glass.
jokes.punchline: His toast is not a celebration but a hedge — 'may tonight be but a minor speed-bump' — framing the bachelor party as a hazard to be survived rather than celebrated.
jokes.explanation: Structurally clever — Phil's toast is simultaneously a celebration and a confession that he expects tonight to be a problem. 'Minor speed-bump' is an understatement that the audience knows (from the opening scene) is ironically prescient. Gets better on rewatch because of dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Hello. How 'bout that ride in. I guess that's why they call it Sin City. Ha-ha-ha.
jokes.setup: Alan stands up to deliver a speech he has prepared. He opens with the confidence of a seasoned public speaker.
jokes.punchline: Alan's opener — 'How 'bout that ride in. I guess that's why they call it Sin City' — is a hacky wedding-speech opening delivered with sincere professionalism, then followed by his own laugh track ('Ha-ha-ha').
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character moment. Alan has prepared a speech with a crowd-warming opener and even rehearsed when to laugh at his own joke. The 'Ha-ha-ha' is what elevates it — Alan performing the audience's reaction for them is a perfect display of his social disconnect. He believes this is how public speaking works. Very high character integration and structure.

jokes.text: You guys might not know this, but I consider myself a bit of a loner. I tend to think of myself as a one-man wolf pack.
jokes.setup: Alan continues his prepared speech. He is sharing a personal insight about himself.
jokes.punchline: The concept of a 'one-man wolf pack' — a pack of one — is both logically contradictory and earnestly delivered as though it's a profound self-understanding.
jokes.explanation: One of the most iconic jokes in the film and among the best in this reel. 'One-man wolf pack' is a logical contradiction that Alan treats as an identity. It encapsulates his loneliness, his self-aggrandizement, his sincerity, and his social blindness simultaneously. The phrase itself became a cultural shorthand. Near-perfect character integration — this is Alan's defining self-description. Very high originality for a character joke.

jokes.text: But when my sister brought Doug home, I knew he was one of my own. And my wolf pack, it grew by one. So there were two of us in the wolf pack. I was alone first in the pack, and then Doug joined in later.
jokes.setup: Alan is emotionally describing how Doug was absorbed into his wolf pack.
jokes.punchline: Alan immediately begins mathematically clarifying the wolf pack membership sequence — 'I was alone first in the pack, and then Doug joined in later' — as though the audience needs an explanation of the chronology of two people.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the wolf pack joke. Alan's need to clarify the chronological record — 'I was alone first' — implies he is worried the audience might think Doug was in the pack before him. The specificity of 'two of us in the wolf pack' as a formal accounting is very funny. Strong character integration and callback structure.

jokes.text: And six months ago, when Doug introduced me to you guys... I thought, 'Wait a second. Could it be?' And now I know for sure. I just added two more guys to my wolf pack. Four of us wolves. Running around the desert together. In Las Vegas. Looking for strippers and cocaine.
jokes.setup: Alan is building emotionally toward welcoming Phil and Stu into his wolf pack.
jokes.punchline: The sentimental arc — 'Could it be? I just added two more' — culminates in a vision of their pack activity: 'Running around the desert together. In Las Vegas. Looking for strippers and cocaine.' Delivered with the same warmth as the preceding sentiment.
jokes.explanation: One of the best sustained jokes in the film. The speech builds with genuine emotional logic — the callback to the wolf pack, the expansion to four — and then the punchline is 'strippers and cocaine' delivered in the same tender tone. The tonal whiplash is perfectly executed. The specificity of 'strippers and cocaine' as a wolf pack's natural pursuits, combined with 'running around the desert' as though they're actual animals, is excellent comedy writing. Near-top score.

jokes.text: And six months ago, when Doug introduced me to you guys... I thought, 'Wait a second. Could it be...?' And now I know for sure. I just added two more guys to my wolf pack.
jokes.setup: Alan has expanded his wolf pack narrative from one to two (himself and Doug). He's now arrived at the present.
jokes.punchline: The 'Could it be...?' moment — Alan's existential suspense before concluding he had found wolf pack members — treats choosing friends with the drama of a religious revelation. The six-month timeline is also funny: he's been living with this question for half a year.
jokes.explanation: Excellent continuation and escalation. 'Could it be...?' with the dramatic pause treats friendship formation as a moment of cosmic discovery. The specificity of 'six months ago' grounds the absurdity in real time — he's been wolf-pack-auditing Phil and Stu for six months before accepting them. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Four of us wolves. Running around the desert together. In Las Vegas. Looking for strippers and cocaine.
jokes.setup: Alan is building the wolf pack image — four wolves, running free in the desert.
jokes.punchline: The noble wolf pack image collapses into 'looking for strippers and cocaine' — the actual Vegas agenda stated with the same earnest gravity as the earlier pack mythology.
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of the wolf pack speech's elevated tone. The fragments — 'Four of us wolves. Running around the desert together. In Las Vegas.' — build a mythic image that is immediately deflated by 'looking for strippers and cocaine,' which is stated with identical solemnity. The bathos is perfectly timed and executed. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: What do you got there? / What the fuck? / What are you doing? / What is that? / Blood brothers.
jokes.setup: Following his toast, Alan has produced something from his satchel. The others react with alarm.
jokes.punchline: Alan's intended follow-through on his brotherhood speech is to cut everyone's hands for a blood brother ritual — which he announces with complete sincerity as 'Blood brothers.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback punchline to the wolf pack speech. Alan has clearly planned this as the ceremonial conclusion — the speech was a lead-up to a blade ritual. The gap between the others' panic and Alan's calm announcement of 'Blood brothers' is the essence of his character. High character integration.

jokes.text: What do you got there? / What the fuck? / What are you doing? / What is that? / Blood brothers. / God damn it. Alan, no. / I'm not doing that. Make him stop.
jokes.setup: Alan has just finished an earnest, beautiful speech about their friendship. He has something in his hand.
jokes.punchline: He pulls out a knife and attempts to perform a blood brother ritual — apparently from his satchel — to formalize the wolf pack. The horror of the other three, while Alan is completely calm, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the wolf pack sequence. Alan's sincere, logical follow-through — if we're wolf pack brothers, we become blood brothers — reveals he had the knife prepared as part of the speech plan. 'Make him stop' from Stu is a great reaction. The satchel payoff (it contained Jägermeister and a knife) is also a nice structural callback. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Alan, come here, buddy. Get in here, crazy. / Alright. To a night the four of us will never forget.
jokes.setup: After the knife incident is resolved, Phil gives the final toast.
jokes.punchline: 'To a night the four of us will never forget' — landing with massive dramatic irony since the audience knows from the opening scene that they will forget everything.
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the reel is structurally perfect in context. The audience has seen the hungover aftermath of this night in the opening minutes — Phil's toast is therefore ironic in a way neither he nor the characters understand. On first viewing it's a good toast with a funny 'get in here, crazy' button; on rewatch it's devastating. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Phil tells Alan to put on pants — twice — in the middle of a tiger crisis
jokes.setup: The room is in chaos: a tiger in the bathroom, everyone panicking
jokes.punchline: Phil's most urgent concern is that Alan is not wearing pants, stated with exasperated calm amid genuine danger
jokes.explanation: Works because the comedic priority inversion — pants over tiger — is perfectly in character for Phil's alpha pragmatism, and the repetition ('I find it a little weird I have to ask twice') adds a layer of genuine irritation that sells the joke.

jokes.text: 'That bitch is gigantic.'
jokes.setup: They've just confirmed a live tiger is in the hotel bathroom
jokes.punchline: Phil's clinical, almost admiring assessment of the tiger's size — 'bitch' used as a gender-neutral intensifier — treats the impossible situation as a spectator sport
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and totally Phil. The word 'bitch' in this context is used with the specific swagger of someone who is simultaneously terrified and trying to seem cool. High quotability.

jokes.text: Alan asked to put on pants: 'Pants, at times like this? I don't have any.'
jokes.setup: Phil repeats his request that Alan put on pants during the tiger emergency
jokes.punchline: Alan treats the absence of pants as a philosophical stance ('at times like this?') before the mundane admission that he literally owns no pants in the suite
jokes.explanation: The two-part joke is well-constructed: 'at times like this?' implies a worldview where pants are optional in emergencies, and then 'I don't have any' punctures any pretension with mundane logistics. Pure Alan.

jokes.text: Stu: 'Hey, Phil, am I missing a tooth?'
jokes.setup: The guys are cataloguing the morning-after disasters: tiger, trashed suite, lost groom
jokes.punchline: Among all the crises, Stu quietly adds that he may be missing a tooth — a bizarrely personal and permanent disaster amid the chaos
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — the missing tooth is personal and irreversible in a way that the tiger or the room damage isn't. The timing, buried amid bigger panics, makes it land as tragicomic for Stu specifically.

jokes.text: Alan, apparently having looked at himself in a mirror: 'I look like a nerdy hillbilly.'
jokes.setup: The group is gathering themselves post-chaos; Alan's appearance is implied to be disheveled
jokes.punchline: Alan's self-assessment is oddly specific and strangely self-aware for a character who is usually oblivious
jokes.explanation: A quick, solid laugh — the specific descriptor 'nerdy hillbilly' is funnier than just 'hillbilly' and Alan's odd self-awareness here is a small comedic beat.

jokes.text: They discover the ringing phone in the suite is Doug's phone — Doug is missing but his phone is here
jokes.setup: Phil calls Doug's cell to find him; Alan says he answered it
jokes.punchline: Alan holds up Doug's phone — it was ringing inside the hotel room, meaning Doug is missing without his phone
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat that gets a laugh — Phil's flat 'No shit' is the comedic seasoning. Functional escalation of the mystery.

jokes.text: 'Whose fuckin' baby is that?'
jokes.setup: The men have already discovered a tiger, a missing groom, and a trashed suite; they open a drawer/find another room
jokes.punchline: A baby. There is now also a baby. Phil's reaction — delivered with identical energy to the tiger reveal — treats this as the logical next horror
jokes.explanation: One of the film's signature escalation jokes. The discovery of a baby after a tiger is structurally perfect — each new revelation has been worse than the last, but the baby subverts that by being simultaneously less dangerous and more legally problematic. The line's economy is flawless: four words, all the right ones. Approaches the 8+ anchor threshold.

jokes.text: Phil: 'Let's go hook up with Doug. We'll deal with the baby later.' Stu: 'Phil, we're not gonna leave a baby in the room.' Phil: 'There's a fucking tiger in the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: The group debates what to do with the baby
jokes.punchline: Phil's attempt to use the tiger as a logical trump card for abandoning the baby — as if one irresponsibility justifies another
jokes.explanation: Phil's logic is hilariously inverted — the tiger isn't a reason to leave the baby, but Phil presents it as if it obviously is. The callback to the tiger functions as a non sequitur that somehow feels like an argument.

jokes.text: Alan: 'Yeah, I gotta side with Stu on this one.'
jokes.setup: Phil and Stu argue about leaving the baby; Alan has been mostly uninvolved
jokes.punchline: Alan weighing in on the side of basic human decency — leaving a baby with a tiger — is funny because Alan is usually the character with the worst judgment
jokes.explanation: Alan's rare moment of moral clarity is funny precisely because he's Alan. Modest laugh.

jokes.text: Alan at breakfast, watching the baby: 'He's jacking his little weenis.' Phil: 'Pull yourself together, man.' Alan: 'Not at the table, Carlos.'
jokes.setup: The men are trying to have a civilized breakfast and work out what happened
jokes.punchline: Alan narrates the baby's innocent self-touching with adult framing, then admonishes 'Carlos' as if he's a naughty dinner guest
jokes.explanation: 'Not at the table, Carlos' is very quotable — Alan's stern parental tone with an unnamed stranger's baby, using the wrong name, is pitch-perfect absurdism. The joke also works on rewatch because we know the baby's name is Tyler.

jokes.text: Phil reads the valet ticket: they checked in at 5:15 AM. Stu: 'Oh, shit. We drove last night?' Phil: 'Driving drunk. Classic.'
jokes.setup: They're reconstructing the previous night from physical clues
jokes.punchline: Phil calls drunk driving 'classic' with the nostalgia of someone recounting a fun tradition, completely unbothered by the criminality
jokes.explanation: Phil's total moral casualness about drunk driving lands as dark comedy. The word 'classic' does enormous work — it implies this is not the first time.

jokes.text: They notice a hospital bracelet on Phil's wrist — Phil was in the hospital last night and doesn't remember it
jokes.setup: The clue-gathering continues; Stu points to Phil's arm
jokes.punchline: Phil was hospitalized and has zero memory of it — another brick in the escalating wall of 'what did we do?'
jokes.explanation: More plot than punchline, but the reveal structure gives it comedic weight. Alan's 'You okay?' followed by Phil's breezy 'Yeah, Alan. I'm fine.' gets a small laugh from Phil's signature nonchalance.

jokes.text: Alan holds the baby up and uses it to mime 'doing a wheelie' or waving — 'Hey, Stu. Watch this.' [baby trick] 'Do you ever see a baby do that?' Phil: 'Alan, it's not cool.'
jokes.setup: Stu is stressed; Alan wants to show off the baby
jokes.punchline: Alan has apparently taught the baby some kind of trick and is performing it, treating the infant like a show dog
jokes.explanation: Alan's relationship with the baby is a consistent source of comedy — his genuine delight in the infant while being completely wrong about how to handle one. Doesn't quite land as well in transcript form; relies heavily on visual.

jokes.text: Alan: 'What are you talkin' about? I've found a baby before.' Phil: 'You've found a baby before?' Alan: 'Yeah.' Phil: 'Where?' Alan: 'Coffee Bean.'
jokes.setup: Stu questions whether Alan is qualified to care for the baby
jokes.punchline: Alan treats finding a baby at a Coffee Bean café as a credential that qualifies him as a baby expert
jokes.explanation: One of the best Alan jokes in the film. The structure is a perfect four-beat interrogation: claim → disbelief → confirmation → specific absurd location. 'Coffee Bean' is the ideal specific detail — not 'a park' or 'a store,' but a mid-tier LA coffee chain, which is simultaneously mundane and deeply weird. The joke implies a whole backstory we never see and don't need to. Fully character-specific to Alan: only he would cite this as experience. Approaches the 8.5 anchor benchmark clearly.

jokes.text: They spot the mattress from Doug's room on the roof of the hotel's marquee/street below, apparently thrown from the window
jokes.setup: They're leaving the hotel when someone spots something strange outside
jokes.punchline: Doug's mattress has been thrown out of the hotel window — another piece of the chaotic night, presented as a mundane discovery
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — the mattress is a physical marker of how out-of-control the night was, but its comedy is primarily visual and contextual rather than verbal.

jokes.text: Bystander explaining the mattress: 'Some assholes threw his bed off the window last night.' Another: 'Some guys just can't handle Vegas.'
jokes.setup: They ask passersby about the mattress on the roof
jokes.punchline: 'Some guys just can't handle Vegas' — a Vegas local treating window-thrown mattresses as a known category of tourist behavior
jokes.explanation: The Vegas-insider attitude toward chaos is a solid observational beat. 'Some guys just can't handle Vegas' works as a knowing Vegas-culture joke — a local shrugging at a mattress on a rooftop.

jokes.text: They return the police car; the valet says 'Here's your car, officers.' They go along with it.
jokes.setup: They've discovered they were driving a stolen police car all night; now they're returning it to the hotel valet
jokes.punchline: The valet treats them as actual officers, which they accept rather than correct — the disguise is inadvertent and they know it
jokes.explanation: Setup for the subsequent cop car jokes; works as cringe-comedy but isn't particularly crafted. The laugh comes from situation more than writing.

jokes.text: Phil accidentally hits the baby with the car door. Bystander: 'You just nailed the baby.' Phil checks his glasses: 'My glasses okay?' Stu: 'Your glasses are fine, dick.'
jokes.setup: Phil is getting into the police car with the baby
jokes.punchline: Phil's first concern after hitting the baby with the door is whether his glasses are okay — Stu calls him a dick, which is correct
jokes.explanation: Phil's narcissistic concern for his glasses over the baby's welfare is both a character joke and a shock joke. 'Your glasses are fine, dick' is a great straight-man line. The beat works because it's the kind of thing you can't quite believe you just saw.

jokes.text: Stu: 'This is so illegal.' Phil: 'Can't you see the fun part of anything?'
jokes.setup: They're driving the stolen police car through Las Vegas with a mystery baby in the back
jokes.punchline: Phil reframes Stu's entirely reasonable concern about federal crime as a failure of imagination
jokes.explanation: Classic Phil/Stu dynamic joke. Phil's moral inversion — framing illegality as a fun deficiency in Stu — is very much his character. The line reads as a genuine worldview rather than a one-off quip.

jokes.text: Stu: 'Yeah we're stuck in traffic in a stolen police car with what is sure to be a missing child in the back seat. Which part of this is fun?' Alan: 'I think the cop car part is pretty cool.' Phil: 'Thank you, Alan. It is cool. Doug would love it.'
jokes.setup: Stu summarizes their situation sarcastically
jokes.punchline: Alan genuinely answers Stu's rhetorical question, and Phil seizes on Alan's validation — 'Doug would love it' is Phil's highest endorsement
jokes.explanation: Three-character interaction that fires on all cylinders: Stu's rhetorical despair, Alan's earnest literal answer, and Phil using Alan-of-all-people as his moral authority. The 'Doug would love it' tag is perfect Phil — it's both a deflection and a character revelation about how he sees Doug.

jokes.text: Phil uses the police PA system: 'Attention, please. Move out of the way. I repeat. Please disperse.' Then: 'Ma'am, in the leopard dress... You have an amazing rack. Get off the sidewalk.'
jokes.setup: They're stuck in traffic in the cop car; Phil grabs the PA microphone
jokes.punchline: Phil starts with an official-sounding police announcement, then pivots to hitting on a woman through the police PA system — the transition is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most memorable bits. The escalation from 'official PA announcement' to 'you have an amazing rack' in the same authoritative cop voice is perfect. Phil's closer — 'Get off the sidewalk' — returning to officious tone after the compliment is structurally excellent. His final line 'I should've been a fuckin' cop' seals the character moment. High quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Doctor conducting Phil's physical exam: 'Alright, come forward. And turn. And cough. Give me one more. Alright. Attaboy. Felix, you can put your robe on.'
jokes.setup: The guys visit the hospital; the doctor is finishing a physical exam on another patient (Felix) while talking to them
jokes.punchline: The audience realizes the doctor has been conducting a prostate/hernia exam — coughing, turning — on an elderly patient while casually conversing with Phil and his friends; 'Attaboy' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Good visual cringe beat — the doctor's clinical cheerfulness during a hernia check ('Attaboy') while multitasking is well-observed comic business. Works better in film than on the page.

jokes.text: Doctor refers to Phil's chart: 'Patient name Phil Wenneck. 2:45 AM arrival. Minor concussion...' Stu: 'Do you mind if I take a look? I'm actually a doctor.' Doctor: 'You said that several times last night. But, really, you're just a dentist.'
jokes.setup: Stu tries to assert professional authority with the hospital doctor
jokes.punchline: The doctor deflates Stu's MD pretension with the same 'just a dentist' diminishment Stu apparently insisted on correcting all night long — it's a callback to Stu's own behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the best Stu jokes in the film. The doctor's 'you said that several times last night' means drunk Stu was loudly claiming to be a real doctor in the ER, only to be shut down then and now. The 'just a dentist' diminishment is devastating because Stu can't argue with someone who was there. Perfect character integration — Stu's status anxiety about being a dentist is a core character trait. Meets the 8+ anchor threshold.

jokes.text: Doctor: 'They found a large amount of Roophyllin in your system.' Stu: 'Roophyllin? Roofies? Commonly known as the Date Rape Drug?' Phil: 'Are you saying I was raped last night?'
jokes.setup: The doctor reveals a drug was found in Phil's bloodwork
jokes.punchline: Phil immediately leaps to 'are you saying I was raped?' — not an unreasonable fear, but delivered with such specificity and self-focus that it's both alarming and funny
jokes.explanation: Dark_subversive territory played through deadpan. Stu's clinical naming of the drug ('commonly known as the Date Rape Drug') plays straight man to Phil's horror. The beat earns its laugh by not softening either character's reaction.

jokes.text: Doctor: 'I wouldn't be worried about it. By now the stuff is out of your system. You're gonna be fine. I have to go.' Phil: 'Wait, please, doctor...' Doctor: 'I'm a doctor, not a tour guide. Figure it out yourself, okay? You're big boys.'
jokes.setup: They ask the doctor if he knows Best Little Chapel's location
jokes.punchline: The doctor's exit line — 'I'm a doctor, not a tour guide' — delivered with the contempt of a man who has tolerated enough, punctuated by 'You're big boys'
jokes.explanation: The doctor's escalating exasperation is well-played. 'I'm a doctor, not a tour guide' is a solid construction — the profession-based refusal — and 'you're big boys' is a perfect condescending dismissal. The specific corner directions ('get a map and fuck off') is the sharper version of this joke.

jokes.text: Doctor's final directions to Best Little Chapel: 'It's on the corner of get a map and fuck off.'
jokes.setup: They ask the doctor where Best Little Chapel is located
jokes.punchline: 'On the corner of get a map and fuck off' — a street-address format used as an insult
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The joke uses a highly specific structural form — street address — to deliver an F-you, making the insult land harder because of its unexpected packaging. 'Corner of get a map and fuck off' is the kind of line that gets repeated outside the film. Economy is nearly perfect: eight words, maximum impact. Comparable to or above the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Phil suggests leaving the baby in the car while they go in: 'Just leave him in the car. We're only gonna be 5 minutes.' Stu: 'We're not leaving a baby in the car.' Phil: 'He'll be fine. I cracked the window.'
jokes.setup: They've arrived at Best Little Chapel and need to go inside
jokes.punchline: 'I cracked the window' — the standard logic applied to dogs applied to a human infant, delivered by Phil with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Phil applying dog-in-hot-car logic to a baby is a brilliant character-specific joke. 'I cracked the window' is the perfect specific detail — not 'he'll be fine' but the precise act of a responsible pet owner. The joke gets a rewatch bonus because on rewatch you appreciate how completely Phil means it.

jokes.text: Eddie the chapel owner to Phil: 'I wanna tell you something. I know some sick people in my life. This guy is the craziest, wildest bastard I ever met in my life... I thought he was gonna eat my dick.'
jokes.setup: They meet the chapel owner, Eddie, who apparently knows them from last night
jokes.punchline: 'I thought he was gonna eat my dick' — the escalation from 'craziest bastard I ever met' to this specific fear as the evidence
jokes.explanation: The euphemistic escalation from 'craziest bastard' to the specific graphic fear is well-timed. Eddie's enthusiasm while recounting something horrifying adds to the charm. The ambiguity of which of them inspired this fear is a secondary comic layer.

jokes.text: Eddie: 'You don't remember nothing?' [pause] 'Congratulations, Stu. You got married.'
jokes.setup: Eddie can barely believe they don't remember their night at his chapel
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'Congratulations, Stu. You got married.' — the film's major reveal of this reel, delivered with all the warmth of a congratulatory greeting card
jokes.explanation: One of the structural pillars of the reel. The pause does real comedic work — the audience and characters have been building to a revelation, and 'Congratulations' is both the word used and the most ironic possible framing. Stu's response ('My life is over') is the perfect button. High impact because it's the moment the audience has been waiting for.

jokes.text: Stu: 'That's it. My life is over.'
jokes.setup: Eddie has just revealed Stu got married last night
jokes.punchline: Stu's immediate verdict — 'my life is over' — delivered as absolute fact, not hyperbole
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Stu's catastrophizing is funny because his girlfriend Melissa is established as controlling, making 'my life is over' feel genuinely accurate rather than dramatic. Functions as a button on joke #32.

jokes.text: Eddie describes the high-roller wedding package: 'You have baseball caps... and fancy calendars, all with pictures of Stu and Jade.' Then describes the bride: 'Clean. Very tight. Tits, like that. But that's because she had a baby.'
jokes.setup: Eddie is showing them the wedding memorabilia
jokes.punchline: Eddie's description of the bride — oscillating between graphic compliment and clinical observation, ending with 'that's because she had a baby' — which retroactively explains the baby they've been carrying
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jade had a baby — and the transition from Eddie's graphic description of her body to this — is structurally a double punchline: the description is funny, then 'that's because she had a baby' is funnier because it explains the Carlos mystery. The rewatch bonus: on second viewing, you've known about Tyler all along.

jokes.text: Eddie describes Jade: '...Tits, like that. But that's because she had a baby.'
jokes.setup: Eddie is describing Stu's new wife to him (since Stu doesn't remember her)
jokes.punchline: Eddie's clinical, unsolicited physical assessment — including the parenthetical baby explanation — is delivered with the casual authority of a used car salesman
jokes.explanation: Eddie's total lack of social filter makes this land. The parenthetical explanation 'because she had a baby' is the best part — an almost scientific aside in an already inappropriate assessment. The setup/callback also pays off when Carlos turns out to be Jade's baby.

jokes.text: 'That explains the baby.' 'Oh, Carlos.' 'Great.'
jokes.setup: Eddie mentions that Jade had a baby
jokes.punchline: The baby mystery is solved; Alan's 'Oh, Carlos' is a callback to his insistence on the wrong name
jokes.explanation: Alan's mourning of the name 'Carlos' is an effective callback payoff. Brief but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Phil: 'I vote we torch the cop car and all the shit with it.' Stu: 'Torch it? Who are you?'
jokes.setup: They need to get rid of evidence of the night; Phil proposes a solution
jokes.punchline: Phil's most extreme possible solution — arson — delivered as a perfectly reasonable suggestion, shocking even Stu
jokes.explanation: Phil's escalating lawlessness throughout this reel is a consistent character joke; torching a cop car is the logical endpoint. 'Who are you?' from Stu functions as the audience surrogate.

jokes.text: Stu: 'I don't know, Phil. Apparently I'm a guy who married a complete stranger.'
jokes.setup: Phil asks Stu who he is (after Stu challenged Phil's identity) — it's a rhetorical slapback
jokes.punchline: Stu's self-deprecating callback to his own situation — the worst possible answer to 'who are you'
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback that integrates the plot. Stu using his own disaster as a rhetorical weapon against Phil is both funny and character-specific. The delivery deflates Phil's moral authority perfectly.

jokes.text: Stu looking at the wedding mementos: 'These mugs. This hat. This car. It's all evidence of a night that never happened. That is why we're torching all of it.'
jokes.setup: Stu has been the voice of caution all reel; now he's converted to Phil's arson plan
jokes.punchline: Stu — the most risk-averse character — has been convinced that torching a police car is the sane option, and delivers this conclusion with the calm logic of a man who has thought it through
jokes.explanation: The character reversal — Stu suddenly becomes the arson advocate — is the joke. The list ('these mugs, this hat, this car') is good setup for the punchline reveal of his conversion.

jokes.text: Stu: 'I'm a school teacher. I got a family. I'm on for secrecy. But I'm not gonna torch a fuckin' cop car.' Phil: 'Fine. I'll do it.' Alan: 'Can I help?' Phil: 'Yeah. Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Stu reverses course again on the torching plan
jokes.punchline: Alan immediately volunteers to help Phil commit arson, and Phil accepts with a sincere 'Thanks' — Alan's enthusiasm for crime and Phil's gratitude both play
jokes.explanation: Alan volunteering for arson with 'Can I help?' as if it's a household chore, and Phil's warm 'Yeah. Thanks.' treating it as a normal team-up, is perfect Alan-Phil comedy. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Stu calls Melissa while standing next to a police car he's about to torch: 'Hey, sweetheart. How are you?' covering their location with winery/sequoia tree lies
jokes.setup: Melissa calls; they're in Las Vegas with a stolen cop car, a mystery baby, and a secret marriage
jokes.punchline: Stu pivots to 'Hey, sweetheart' with the ease of a man who has been lying to Melissa for years — the contrast between the chaos and his breezy performance is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — audience knows everything Stu is hiding. The 'sequoia trees' excuse is specific enough to be funny; Melissa's 'I hate that' (re the reception) is a small character reveal.

jokes.text: Stu on the phone with Melissa, covering their tracks: 'We're on all kind of vino factoids.' Then: 'So cool if I could breast-feed, you know.'
jokes.setup: Stu is improvising a fake story about being at a winery on a wine tour
jokes.punchline: 'So cool if I could breast-feed, you know' — a non sequitur that makes no sense in the winery cover story context, apparently improvised on the spot
jokes.explanation: Stu's lie unraveling in real time — 'breast-feed' clearly triggered by the baby in front of him — is both a cringe joke about bad improvisation and a Freudian slip joke. The specificity of 'breast-feed' as the tell is inspired.

jokes.text: Stu covers the breast-feed slip with 'We're about to go for a tractor ride. So I should probably get going.' Melissa: 'A tractor ride?'
jokes.setup: Stu needs to explain away the breast-feeding comment
jokes.punchline: His cover story — a tractor ride — is so mundane and random that Melissa's confused 'A tractor ride?' sells how thin the lie is
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe beat that shows Stu's desperation; works mainly as connective tissue in the phone call sequence.

jokes.text: During the phone call, the cop car 'backfires' (is apparently set on fire); Phil shouts in background; Stu covers: 'What was that? They just started up the tractor. I think it backfired.'
jokes.setup: Phil is torching the police car while Stu talks to Melissa on the phone
jokes.punchline: The sound of a car being set on fire is explained away as a tractor backfire — the least convincing lie in the sequence
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation on the phone lie sequence — each cover story gets worse. The tractor callback is the logical if strained endpoint.

jokes.text: Chinese gangsters appear in a car demanding Eddie: 'Where the fuck are you? Is that a baby?' Stu: 'Why does it have to be a baby? We're in a winery. It's a goat.'
jokes.setup: Chinese gangsters interrupt to look for someone; Stu is simultaneously on the phone with Melissa
jokes.punchline: Stu insists the baby is a goat, maintaining his winery cover story to Melissa in the face of a threat; the lie is for Melissa, not the gangster, making it doubly absurd
jokes.explanation: Brilliant multi-layered joke: Stu is being threatened by armed gangsters and his primary concern is that Melissa on the phone doesn't know there's a baby. The 'it's a goat' — which is insane to tell a gangster — only makes sense as a continuation of the winery lie for Melissa's benefit. The audience simultaneously gets the gangster threat, the phone lie, and Stu's scrambled priorities. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: In the middle of the gangster standoff and gunshots, Stu simply says: 'I gotta call you back.'
jokes.setup: Gangsters shoot Eddie; chaos erupts; they flee
jokes.punchline: Stu ends the phone call with his girlfriend with the most mundane signoff possible while gangsters are shooting people around him
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. 'I gotta call you back' during a drive-by shooting is the perfect Stu joke: his reflex is still managing Melissa's feelings even in mortal peril. Economy is nearly perfect — there is no world where more words improve this. Meets the 8+ anchor benchmark clearly.

jokes.text: Phil driving away after the shooting: 'Why don't you just let that one go to voice mail?' [about Melissa calling back]
jokes.setup: Melissa is apparently calling back after being hung up on during the shooting
jokes.punchline: Phil suggests voicemail as the solution to being shot at, with the calm tone of someone advising on call management
jokes.explanation: Phil's perpetual unfazedness gets another clean expression. The specificity of 'let that one go to voicemail' as post-shooting advice is perfectly Phil.

jokes.text: Alan, apparently watching something on the car's police laptop/screen: 'That's a fake laugh, by the way.' Then: 'It's got Ted Danson and Magnum P.I. and that Jewish actor.'
jokes.setup: They're in a car fleeing a gunfight; Alan is watching what appears to be a TV show on the police computer
jokes.punchline: Alan has found a show on the police car's computer — immediately after being shot at — and is critiquing the laugh track and listing the cast
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Alan. While fleeing a shooting, Alan has found a TV show and is engaged in leisurely media criticism — 'that's a fake laugh' — and his description 'that Jewish actor' is a great Alan non-specificity (he can't remember the name). Character-perfect absurdism.

jokes.text: Phil: 'Did you hear that? The baby's name is Tyler.' Alan: 'I thought he looked more like a Carlos too, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Jade reveals the baby's name is Tyler; Alan had been calling him Carlos all reel
jokes.punchline: Alan's consolation to Phil ('I thought he looked more like a Carlos too, buddy') presumes that Phil also preferred Carlos — which he didn't — and treats a baby's actual name as a matter of preference
jokes.explanation: Perfect Carlos callback payoff. Alan's 'I thought he looked more like a Carlos too, buddy' — the 'too' implying shared opinion, the 'buddy' as consolation — is very character-specific to Alan's oblivious solidarity. Great economy.

jokes.text: 'Did you hear that? The baby's name is Tyler.' / 'I thought he looked more like a Carlos too, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Jade reveals the baby's real name is Tyler
jokes.punchline: Alan laments that the real name doesn't suit the baby — aligning himself with 'Carlos' over the actual name; Phil comforts him by validating his wrong choice
jokes.explanation: Phil's gentle 'I thought he looked more like a Carlos too, buddy' is a surprisingly warm joke — he's consoling Alan about the wrong baby name the same way you'd console a child who gave the wrong answer. The Carlos gag has been well-maintained across the reel and this is a satisfying warm-callback.

jokes.text: Jade is breast-feeding Tyler while talking to them. Phil: 'Holy shit.' Stu: 'She is super hot. You should be proud of yourself.'
jokes.setup: Jade has excused herself to feed the baby; apparently does so in front of them
jokes.punchline: Phil's honest shock and Stu's immediate pivot to pride — 'you should be proud of yourself' — are both very character-specific reactions to seeing your friend's new wife
jokes.explanation: Modest laugh. Stu's friend-complimenting-friend tone ('you should be proud') about an accidental drunken marriage is a solid character beat.

jokes.text: Alan: 'I didn't know they gave out rings at the holocaust.'
jokes.setup: Stu explains it's his grandmother's 'holocaust ring'
jokes.punchline: Alan takes the word 'holocaust ring' literally — as if it's a ring distributed at the Holocaust — revealing his total historical ignorance
jokes.explanation: One of the great Alan lines. The joke works on a narrow but perfect misunderstanding: Stu means 'a ring belonging to a holocaust survivor,' Alan hears 'a ring from the holocaust.' The sincerity is what makes it land — Alan isn't making a dark joke, he genuinely didn't know. His complete historical obliviousness is both funny and in character. Dark but not mean-spirited in context. High quotability, strong economy, exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Stu: 'She is wearing my grandmother's ring. The ring I'm gonna give to Melissa. Remember my grandmother's holocaust ring?' Alan: 'I didn't know they give out rings at the holocaust.'
jokes.setup: Stu notices Jade is wearing a family ring he was saving for his proposal to Melissa
jokes.punchline: Alan's completely literal misunderstanding of what a 'holocaust ring' is — processing it as a commemorative event gift rather than a family heirloom — is both darkly funny and reveals Alan's profound ignorance
jokes.explanation: One of the best Alan jokes in the film. The joke works on multiple levels: Alan's obliviousness is established but this plumbs new depths; his parsing of 'holocaust ring' as 'ring given at the holocaust' implies a vast and disturbing ignorance; and the matter-of-fact delivery makes it land as a genuine question rather than a provocation. The specificity of 'give out rings' — as if it were a party favor — is what makes it exceptional. Character-specific in the deepest possible way. Comparable to or slightly above the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Jade: 'You know this. I'm a stripper. Technically I'm an escort, but stripping is a great way to meet the clients.'
jokes.setup: Alan asks if Jade is a nurse or blackjack dealer; she corrects him
jokes.punchline: Jade's matter-of-fact business logic — stripping as a client acquisition strategy for escorting — delivered as obvious professional wisdom
jokes.explanation: Jade's total lack of shame and her framing of prostitution as a professional pipeline is perfectly delivered. The structure of the sentence — the correction ('technically an escort') followed by the business logic ('stripping is a great way to meet clients') — sounds like a LinkedIn profile summary. Very quotable. Alan's 'Smart. / Savvy.' double-word endorsement is the kicker.

jokes.text: Stu: 'But that's all in the past now that I'm marrying a doctor.' Phil/Stu: 'I'm just a dentist.'
jokes.setup: Jade explains she's a stripper-escort but it's fine now that she's marrying a doctor (Stu)
jokes.punchline: Stu reflexively corrects 'doctor' to 'just a dentist' — his status self-deprecation resurfaces at the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the 'just a dentist' joke from the hospital. The situation is now reversed — a stripper is claiming him as a doctor, which Stu should welcome — but his instinct to correct 'doctor' to 'just a dentist' is so ingrained that he does it anyway, even when it works against him. This is Stu's funniest character moment in the reel precisely because it's so involuntary. Meets 8+ threshold.

jokes.text: Police burst in to arrest them: 'Police. Freeze! Shut that baby up.'
jokes.setup: Stu has just been told his wife is a stripper-escort and corrected his own professional title
jokes.punchline: The scene is immediately interrupted by police arresting everyone — the timing punctuates Stu's humiliation with a new, worse disaster
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat — the arrest is both plot and comedy, arriving at the perfect moment of maximum Stu embarrassment. 'Shut that baby up' as a police command is a small additional laugh.
