jokes.text: Police officer shows tourists around the holding area: 'Trust me, kids. You do not want to be sitting on these benches. We call this place Loserville.'
jokes.setup: Phil, Stu, and Alan are being processed at the police station; a cop is leading a tour
jokes.punchline: The cop is giving a tour of the holding area while our heroes are being processed as the losers in 'Loserville' — they are literal exhibits in this lesson
jokes.explanation: Good contextual irony — the guys are literally the cautionary tale. 'Loserville' is a decent line but the visual of them being processed while kids are warned about their exact bench is funnier in film than on paper.

jokes.text: Phil calls Tracy and lies: 'We are at the spa, at the hotel.' Tracy: 'Is Doug around?' Phil: 'Of course he's around. Why wouldn't he be around? I'm just wondering why you're calling me.'
jokes.setup: Phil calls Doug's fiancée Tracy to manage her expectations; Doug has been missing for 12+ hours
jokes.punchline: Phil's aggressive deflection — 'why wouldn't he be around? I'm just wondering why you're calling me' — goes on offense to avoid answering a simple question
jokes.explanation: Phil's confident lying under impossible circumstances is consistent character work. The escalating defensiveness ('why wouldn't he be around?') is very Phil.

jokes.text: Police officer reveals the found Mercedes: 'There's also a note. It says, couldn't find the meter, but here's 4 bucks.'
jokes.setup: The officer is telling them their car was found abandoned in the middle of Las Vegas Boulevard
jokes.punchline: Drunk Phil (or one of them) left a $4 parking note on a luxury Mercedes abandoned in traffic — the civility of the gesture against the lawlessness of the action
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best written jokes. The $4 note is a perfect detail — specific enough to feel real, polite enough to be absurd, cheap enough ($4 for a Mercedes?) to be funny. The idea that drunk them followed parking meter protocol with $4 while blocking Las Vegas Boulevard is inspired. The note implies a character — considerate enough to leave money, oblivious enough to think this helps.

jokes.text: Phil: 'We didn't steal anything. We found it. If anything, we deserve a reward or something. Like a trophy?'
jokes.setup: Detective says they can't be released because they stole a police car
jokes.punchline: Phil reframes grand theft auto as a good deed worthy of recognition — specifically requesting a trophy
jokes.explanation: Phil's moral inversion is at peak form here. 'We found it' is the thinnest possible defense; asking for 'a reward or something — like a trophy?' is Phil's ego making a truly unhinged request. The 'like a trophy?' escalation is what makes it — he's not joking, he genuinely thinks this argument will work.

jokes.text: Police officer ranting: 'I see assholes like you everyday. Every fuckin' day. Let's go to Vegas. We all get drunk and laid. Let's steal a cop car, 'cause it'll be really fuckin' funny. Think you can get away with it? Not up in here! Not up in here!'
jokes.setup: The officer is lecturing Phil, Stu, and Alan about stealing the police car
jokes.punchline: 'Not up in here! Not up in here!' — the officer's rant escalates from sensible to unhinged, ending with an oddly specific catchphrase that is more threatening-parent than police authority
jokes.explanation: The officer's rant is a good bit — his ventriloquism of the tourists' thought process ('Let's steal a cop car, cause it'll be really fuckin' funny') shows he's done this speech before. 'Not up in here' repeated twice is the unhinged button that sells it.

jokes.text: Phil begins negotiating with the officer: 'If I may. I'm assuming that squad car belongs to one of you.' Officer: 'Yeah.' Phil: 'I'm not a cop. I'm no hero. I'm a school teacher. But if one of my kids went missing on a field trip, that looked really bad on me.'
jokes.setup: Phil attempts to negotiate their release by appealing to the officer's professional ego
jokes.punchline: Phil positions himself as a helpless school teacher to gain sympathy, then uses the missing-kid-on-field-trip analogy to appeal to the officer's professional reputation — it's a purely cynical manipulation delivered as heartfelt
jokes.explanation: Phil is at his best when deploying charm in service of selfishness. The school teacher persona is funny because it's so incongruous with everything we've seen him do. His 'I'm no hero' is perfectly disingenuous. The analogy is slippery enough to almost make sense, which is the point.

jokes.text: Phil's negotiation tactic: 'I'm not a cop. I'm no hero. I'm a school teacher. But if one of my kids went missing on a field trip... that would look really bad on me.'
jokes.setup: Phil attempts to negotiate their release; everyone waits to hear his argument
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'argument' is that losing a student on a field trip would be embarrassing for him — the most self-serving possible framing of 'help us find our friend'
jokes.explanation: Phil's rhetorical strategy is to make his own problem the detective's problem — but the argument he constructs is entirely self-interested ('it would look bad on me') rather than actually humanitarian. His logic is simultaneously transparent and confident. The setup ('I'm not a cop. I'm no hero.') makes it sound like a moment of humility before it pivots to pure Phil. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Officer cheerfully announces the guys are 'in for a real treat' — which turns out to be being tased by schoolchildren
jokes.setup: Officer asks if anyone has heart conditions, building anticipation with bureaucratic seriousness
jokes.punchline: The 'real treat' is that the men will be tased in front of a class as a demonstration
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the clinical formality of the heart-condition question primes the audience for something scary, then reframes it as a school demonstration, which makes the humiliation worse. The 'real treat' line lands because of dramatic irony the men haven't caught yet.

jokes.text: 'Not you, fat Jesus. Slide it on back.'
jokes.setup: Officer asks for a volunteer to shoot the stun gun; Alan eagerly steps forward
jokes.punchline: Officer dismisses Alan with the nickname 'fat Jesus' — a callback to Alan's Jesus-like beard/appearance — and picks 'pretty boy' instead
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. 'Fat Jesus' is an inspired, specific, visual nickname for Zach Galifianakis's Alan — it captures exactly what his character looks like and immediately becomes quotable. Delivered with total nonchalance by the officer, maximizing the deadpan. Economy is near-perfect: three words do enormous work.

jokes.text: 'Right in the nuts. That was beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Stu shoots Phil with the stun gun
jokes.punchline: The officer's clinical aesthetic appreciation — 'beautiful' — for a shot to the groin is perfectly wrong-toned
jokes.explanation: The officer treating a nut-shot with the reverence of a golf commentator is a solid deadpan bit. Economy is excellent — just five words. The groin shot itself is an older gag but the delivery elevates it.

jokes.text: Officer calls Alan up to shoot — Alan, the most dangerous possible person, gets handed a weapon
jokes.setup: Officer says there's one charge left and asks for a volunteer; the audience knows Alan is unhinged
jokes.punchline: Officer chooses Alan ('big man') — the worst possible outcome — escalating the stakes comedically
jokes.explanation: Works on dramatic irony — the audience's knowledge of Alan's character creates dread-anticipation. The payoff (he shoots the officer in the face) is the real joke, but this setup moment earns its own laugh.

jokes.text: 'You're holding 50,000 volts, little man. Don't be afraid to ride the lightning.'
jokes.setup: Alan stands intensely with the stun gun; officer coaches him
jokes.punchline: Calling the heavyset, wild-eyed Alan 'little man' and telling him to 'ride the lightning' is simultaneously condescending and unintentionally ominous
jokes.explanation: 'Little man' applied to Alan is a visual gag through dialogue — the officer is oblivious to what he's about to unleash. 'Ride the lightning' is a great phrase that becomes retroactively funny when Alan shoots him in the face.

jokes.text: Alan shoots the officer in the face
jokes.setup: Alan has been coached to shoot at the suspect (Phil); instead he turns and shoots the officer giving the demonstration
jokes.punchline: 'In the face.' — Alan tases the cop running the show, right in the face
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff: the entire stun-gun sequence has been building to Alan doing something wrong, and shooting the authority figure in the face is the ideal subversion. 'In the face' as the sole caption is devastating economy. Character-perfect — Alan would absolutely do this. High rewatch value as the audience anticipates it on second viewing.

jokes.text: 'He's still up.' — the officer is still standing after the face tase
jokes.setup: Alan shoots the officer in the face with 50,000 volts
jokes.punchline: The officer doesn't go down immediately — the matter-of-fact observation 'He's still up' treats it like a sporting event
jokes.explanation: Good beat that extends the joke — the officer's resilience is a secondary punchline. 'He's still up' has the economy and sportscaster framing that works, though it's a supporting gag rather than a headliner.

jokes.text: 'Somebody's big boys. You gotta give them two shots.'
jokes.setup: The officer has just been shot in the face and needs a second charge to go down
jokes.punchline: He casually explains, as if still teaching a class, that large men need two tase shots — turning his own incapacitation into a pedagogical moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — the officer maintains his professorial composure even while being tased, turning his own collapse into a lesson about body mass. The commitment to the bit is what elevates this above a simple reaction gag.

jokes.text: 'Fuck those guys. Do you hear me? That was bullshit. I'm telling everybody we stole a cop car.'
jokes.setup: The cops have let them go after the stun gun demonstration
jokes.punchline: Stu's indignation at 'police brutality' — while simultaneously threatening to confess to a crime — perfectly reveals his skewed priorities and impotent rage
jokes.explanation: Stu threatening to tell everyone they stole a cop car as his form of revenge is a great character beat — his self-righteous fury has no logical exit. The irony that this 'revenge' would only hurt them is well-integrated.

jokes.text: 'One man doesn't shut up. Jesus Christ.'
jokes.setup: Stu has been ranting about police brutality as they walk away from the police station
jokes.punchline: Phil's exhausted aside to no one in particular — 'one man doesn't shut up' — delivered while Stu is still going
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat that characterizes Phil's weary straight-man role. Not extraordinary but lands as a small punctuation to Stu's rant.

jokes.text: 'I was so upset when my grandpa died… How did he die? World War II… Die in battle? No, he was skiing in Vermont. It was just during World War II.'
jokes.setup: Alan is tearfully worried about Doug, mentions losing people he was close to — specifically his grandfather dying in World War II
jokes.punchline: Phil asks if he died in battle; Alan clarifies he was skiing in Vermont — the war is entirely incidental, the death is mundane
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film. The setup is a perfect fake-out: Alan says his grandfather died in World War II, which any audience will read as a heroic combat death, warranting genuine respect. The pivot to 'skiing in Vermont' is a complete non-sequitur that makes the WWII detail absurdly meaningless — he just happened to die during WWII. This is excellent misdirection with layers: it's also character-perfect for Alan to bring up a completely irrelevant grievance in a moment of genuine emotion. The structure is airtight, the punchline is unexpected, and it rewards the second beat (Phil's confused follow-up) beautifully. Approaches the calibration anchor for 8+ moments.

jokes.text: 'I'll tell you another thing. 6 to 1 odds are our car is beat to shit.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing their missing friend and trying to stay calm
jokes.punchline: Stu's first instinct, in a moment of emotional gravity, is to pivot to gambling odds about the state of their car
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Stu's anxious deflection into hyper-specific worry (6 to 1 odds) is consistent with his character. Functional humor that serves the scene more than it stands alone.

jokes.text: 'Oh, shit. I can't see that.' / 'I'm not looking.'
jokes.setup: They approach and open their car, expecting damage
jokes.punchline: Both men immediately avert their eyes upon seeing the car's interior — the visual disgust reaction before we (or they) know what it is
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — their immediate physical revulsion without explanation teases the audience and sets up the inventory of disgusting car discoveries. The 'I'm not looking' as a resigned statement of fact is a small gem of delivery.

jokes.text: 'I found a black shoe… A women's shoe? I don't know. It's men's size 6. It's weird.'
jokes.setup: They're searching the car for clues about what happened the night before
jokes.punchline: A men's size 6 shoe — tiny, unexplained, possibly cross-dressing — is the least of their problems but gets its own solemn analysis
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist escalation in the car-inventory sequence. The specificity of 'men's size 6' and the grave 'it's weird' are well-timed beats in a good running gag.

jokes.text: 'What is this, a snake skin?' / 'Oh, come on. That's a used condom, Alan.'
jokes.setup: Alan holds up an unidentified object during the car inventory
jokes.punchline: Alan's genuine inability to identify a condom — asking if it's snakeskin — reveals extraordinary naïveté; Phil's weary correction lands the joke
jokes.explanation: Very good character-based joke. Alan's misidentification isn't random — it's character-consistent innocence/obliviousness that makes him Alan. Phil's flat correction ('Oh, come on. That's a used condom, Alan') is perfect straight-man delivery. The name 'Alan' at the end of the correction adds extra pathos.

jokes.text: 'I got a jizz on me.'
jokes.setup: Alan is handling the used condom and trying to get it out of the car
jokes.punchline: Alan announces, with the same gravity one might use for 'I've been shot,' that he has gotten semen on himself
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'I got a jizz on me' — using 'a jizz' as a countable noun — is the actual joke. It's a malapropism that reveals Alan's unusual relationship with language. The deadpan delivery of a gross-out moment elevates it above pure shock comedy. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: They discover something is in the trunk; they cautiously open it and a naked Asian man jumps out and attacks them
jokes.setup: The group heard a noise from the trunk and assumes it must be their missing friend Doug
jokes.punchline: Instead of Doug, a screaming, naked Asian man (Mr. Chow) explodes out of the trunk swinging a crowbar
jokes.explanation: One of the most effective shock-comedy moments in the film. The setup is perfect — 'Doug's in the trunk' builds genuine hope and tension — making the violent, naked, screaming surprise all the more explosive. The escalating dread of opening the trunk followed by pure chaotic violence is well-constructed. Very high impact even on rewatch due to the craft of the misdirection.

jokes.text: 'I hate Godzilla. I hate him too. He destroys cities.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Chow has just attacked them and is disoriented; Phil tries to calm him down
jokes.punchline: Phil agrees that Godzilla is bad and 'destroys cities' — both men bonding over their hatred of Godzilla as a de-escalation tactic while a naked man holds a crowbar
jokes.explanation: Brilliant absurdist de-escalation. Phil's tactic of immediately agreeing with the deranged naked man's Godzilla hatred — and both characters earnestly discussing why Godzilla is bad ('he destroys cities') — is surreal and character-revealing. It shows Phil's street-smart adaptability. Very quotable, works independently as a joke.

jokes.text: 'This isn't your fault. I'll get you some pants.'
jokes.setup: Phil is calming down Mr. Chow, who has just emerged naked from a trunk in a violent rage
jokes.punchline: Phil's offer to get him pants — the most practical and least relevant response to a man who just attacked them with a crowbar — delivered with gentle sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — 'I'll get you some pants' is the smallest possible response to an enormous situation. The gentleness of 'this isn't your fault' followed by the mundane solution of pants is an inspired comic beat. Phil treating a surreal hostage situation like a minor inconvenience is funny and character-consistent.

jokes.text: 'I have an internal bleeding. Please call 911.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Chow has just attacked them all and caused chaos jumping out of the trunk
jokes.punchline: He now calmly asks them to call 911 for his internal bleeding — presenting himself as the victim after attacking them
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for Mr. Chow — his immediate pivot to victim status after brutal violence is funny and consistent with his later characterization as narcissistic and self-serving. 'I have AN internal bleeding' is also a small grammatical quirk that adds to his voice.

jokes.text: Alan confesses he 'slipped something' in their Jägermeister — roofies he thought were ecstasy, bought from a dealer at a liquor store
jokes.setup: The men realize their blackout was drugged — Alan begins his confession gravely
jokes.punchline: He drugged them with roofies he thought were ecstasy, bought from 'the guy at the liquor store'
jokes.explanation: Major revelation that recontextualizes the entire film — Alan drugged his new friends on purpose to 'help everyone have a good time.' This is both a plot bomb and a comedy bomb. The escalating specificity (he 'used to do 3 hits a night') deepens the horror and the hilarity. High impact because it changes everything retroactively.

jokes.text: 'I used to do 3 hits at night.'
jokes.setup: Alan is confessing he gave them one hit each of what he thought was ecstasy
jokes.punchline: His casual aside that he personally used to take three hits — said as though this is a normal thing to volunteer — deepens the portrait of Alan as genuinely unhinged
jokes.explanation: One of Alan's best character jokes. The confidence and implied pride with which he mentions his personal dosage — as though that's a point in his favor — is pitch-perfect character comedy. Economy is excellent: six words that say everything about Alan.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry. You mean the drug dealer at the liquor store wasn't a good guy?'
jokes.setup: Alan defends his drug source: 'The guy I bought it from seemed like he was a real straight shooter'
jokes.punchline: Phil's withering sarcasm — 'you mean the drug dealer at the liquor store wasn't a good guy?' — exposes the absurdity of Alan's trust with perfect economy
jokes.explanation: Phil's dry sarcasm hits perfectly here. 'The drug dealer at the liquor store wasn't a good guy' — repeating Alan's setup back at him with incredulity — is an efficient, funny line that also characterizes both men precisely. Highly quotable, clean structure, earns its laugh.

jokes.text: 'He drugged us. I lost a tooth. I married a whore.'
jokes.setup: Stu is furious about Alan drugging them and listing the consequences
jokes.punchline: The escalating list climaxes with 'I married a whore' — delivered with the same weight as losing a tooth, implying marriage is worse than dental trauma
jokes.explanation: Excellent list joke. The rule of three (he drugged us / I lost a tooth / I married a whore) is perfect structurally, and 'I married a whore' landing as a matter-of-fact grievance equal in weight to dental loss is funny and character-defining for Stu. The economy is surgical. One of the reel's strongest lines.

jokes.text: 'How dare you. She's a nice lady.'
jokes.setup: Stu calls the woman he accidentally married a 'whore'
jokes.punchline: Alan, who enabled all of this, indignantly defends a stripper/escort's honor — with Victorian propriety — against the man she just inadvertently married
jokes.explanation: Alan's misplaced gallantry is a great character beat — he is both responsible for the disaster and the most offended by the language used to describe it. 'She's a nice lady' delivered with offended dignity is a quotable line.

jokes.text: 'Our best friend Doug is probably face down in a ditch right now with a meth head butt-fucking his corpse.'
jokes.setup: Phil has tried to find a silver lining in Alan's revelation; Stu sarcastically agrees it's 'totally a good thing'
jokes.punchline: Stu's hyperbolically dark scenario for Doug's fate — delivered at peak emotional intensity — is so outrageously specific it becomes absurd
jokes.explanation: Stu's escalating catastrophizing reaches genuinely dark absurdist territory here. The specificity ('meth head, butt-fucking his corpse') is what makes it funny rather than just gross — it's so hyper-detailed it reads as parody of worst-case-scenario thinking. Phil's dry 'that's highly unlikely' is an excellent straight-man button.

jokes.text: 'You are literally too stupid to insult.' / 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Alan cheerfully explains that memory loss is 'one of the side-effects of roofies' — helpfully, as though this is new information
jokes.punchline: Stu tells Alan he's too stupid to insult; Alan thanks him, completely missing the insult
jokes.explanation: One of the best Alan jokes in the film. The structure is airtight: Stu escalates to the ultimate insult ('too stupid to insult'), which Alan interprets as a compliment. The 'Thank you' is perfectly timed and character-perfect — Alan isn't performing innocence, he genuinely does not understand. The joke is completely character-integrated and would not work with any other character. Economy is superb — four words between setup and payoff.

jokes.text: 'Did we leave the music on?'
jokes.setup: They return to their hotel suite, which has been ominously quiet until they hear sound from inside
jokes.punchline: Phil's mundane, oblivious first instinct ('did we leave the music on?') when the audience — and by now Phil himself — should know something far weirder is in there
jokes.explanation: Good beat that functions as the calm before the Mike Tyson storm. The normality of the question — 'did we leave the music on' — has an absurdist quality because nothing in this hotel room has been normal. Works well on rewatch when you know what's playing.

jokes.text: They open the door to find Mike Tyson in their suite, singing along to Phil Collins' 'In the Air Tonight' with headphones on
jokes.setup: The source of the music turns out to be a person — the last person anyone would expect
jokes.punchline: Mike Tyson, in their hotel suite, completely lost in a tender moment with Phil Collins — drumming the air, eyes closed, fully committed
jokes.explanation: One of the great comedic reveals in modern Hollywood film. The incongruity is pitch-perfect: Mike Tyson — the most feared boxer alive, a man associated with controlled ferocity — singing Phil Collins in a private tender moment in a stranger's hotel suite. The genius is that Tyson IS genuinely enjoying himself, which makes it both funny and oddly sweet. The choice of 'In the Air Tonight' (famous drum fill) is perfect — it has its own emotional weight that creates a surreal tonal collision. This is what a 9+ craft score looks like: original, structurally perfect, works on multiple levels, and becomes a cultural moment.

jokes.text: 'This is my favorite part coming in right now.' / points to chorus / 'The chorus line, guys. Oh, Lord.'
jokes.setup: Tyson is in their suite listening to Phil Collins; he notices them and instead of being menacing, shares his enthusiasm for the song
jokes.punchline: Tyson acts as a music tour guide — 'this is my favorite part' — with the excited energy of someone sharing their passion, not the energy of someone who is about to destroy them
jokes.explanation: The extension of the Tyson gag — him narrating his favorite parts — adds layers to what could have been a one-beat joke. Tyson becomes a character, not just a cameo shock. 'The chorus line, guys. Oh, Lord.' is delivered with genuine music-lover reverence. The comedy here comes from unexpected tenderness from an unexpected source, which is a sophisticated comedic mechanism.

jokes.text: Tyson punches Alan squarely in the face when asked why the tiger is in the bathroom
jokes.setup: Tyson's translator asks why his tiger is in their bathroom; Phil tries to explain diplomatically
jokes.punchline: Before the explanation is complete, Tyson just punches Alan in the face — sudden, complete, with no warning
jokes.explanation: Perfect physical comedy moment. The beat works because: (1) Alan is the wrong person to punch — he's not the one who tried to explain; (2) it's instant and total — no escalation, no warning; (3) it's Mike Tyson, so the punch has iconic weight. Economy is essentially perfect — the action says everything. The incongruity of the tender Phil Collins scene followed immediately by a face punch is a great structural juxtaposition.

jokes.text: 'Hold on. That was completely unnecessary. I'm a huge fan. When you knocked out Holmes—' / 'Explain.'
jokes.setup: Alan has just been punched in the face by Mike Tyson
jokes.punchline: His first post-punch response is to protest the punch is 'unnecessary,' immediately pivot to being a fan, and start citing fight history — while bleeding, to a translator, as if the translator is Tyson
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Alan's recovery from a Tyson punch is to essentially try to network. The 'Explain' interruption by the translator cutting off Alan mid-fanboy moment is a sharp button.

jokes.text: 'And if you wanna kill us, just go ahead, because I don't even care anymore.'
jokes.setup: Stu is explaining their situation to the translator/Tyson — they were drugged, lost their friend, married a stranger
jokes.punchline: Stu's total existential surrender — 'just kill us, I don't care' — delivered with genuine emotional exhaustion
jokes.explanation: Stu's nihilistic resignation is funny because it's completely earned by this point in the film. The death wish in front of a person who actually could kill him adds a darkly comic edge. Good character moment.

jokes.text: 'That's Doug's.' / 'Yeah. Doug. His wallet and his room keys in there.' / 'That's our missing friend.' / 'I don't give a fuck.'
jokes.setup: They identify the jacket found in Tyson's tiger cage as Doug's — this proves Doug was alive
jokes.punchline: Tyson's translator (or Tyson via translator) flatly says 'I don't give a fuck' — a complete dismissal of their emotional breakthrough
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation joke. Their genuine excitement about a clue is immediately torpedoed by Tyson's complete disinterest. 'I don't give a fuck' is perfect economy for the indifferent celebrity.

jokes.text: 'Maybe the tiger would ate them up like Omar.' / 'What happened to Omar?' / 'Don't worry about Omar. He's not with us no more.'
jokes.setup: Tyson speculates that if he'd been awake, the men wouldn't have been able to take his tiger
jokes.punchline: The casual aside about 'Omar,' who was apparently eaten by the tiger, delivered as a matter-of-fact non-answer ('he's not with us no more')
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient — 'Don't worry about Omar. He's not with us no more' implies a person was eaten by this tiger, delivered as casual housekeeping. The nonchalance is the joke. Good dark comedy beat that expands the tiger's threat level retroactively.

jokes.text: 'We're not gonna put it in the Bentley. You brought it here, you bring it back.'
jokes.setup: The plan is established to return the tiger to Tyson's property
jokes.punchline: The practical problem of tiger transportation is solved by telling the guys they have to drive the tiger back themselves in their car
jokes.explanation: Good pragmatic joke — 'you brought it here, you bring it back' as a rule applied to a live tiger is funny. The Bentley specification adds class-contrast comedy. Sets up the driving-with-the-tiger sequence.

jokes.text: 'That was Mike Tyson.' / 'No shit that was Mike Tyson.' / 'I'm just saying, he's still got it.'
jokes.setup: They've just had the entire Tyson encounter, including Alan being punched in the face
jokes.punchline: Alan's takeaway from being punched by Mike Tyson is that Tyson 'still has it' — a boxing fan's appreciative commentary on his own assault
jokes.explanation: Perfect Alan character joke. His sports-commentary assessment of his own face-punch — 'he's still got it' — is both oblivious and strangely admiring. It's also meta-aware in a funny way: Alan has actually verified Tyson's power firsthand. Very character-integrated and quotable.

jokes.text: They play rock-paper-scissors to decide who has to put the steak in with the tiger; Stu loses
jokes.setup: Someone has to go into the bathroom with a live tiger to deliver a drugged steak
jokes.punchline: The world's most dangerous errand is decided by rock-paper-scissors — and then Phil refuses to override the result even though he could
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the tiger feeding sequence. Phil's refusal to override — 'it's rock-paper-scissors, there's nothing more fair' — is a good character beat that reveals his slightly selfish streak.

jokes.text: 'Why are you peppering the steak. You don't know if tigers like pepper.' / 'Tigers love pepper. They hate cinnamon.'
jokes.setup: They are preparing a drugged steak to knock out the tiger
jokes.punchline: Alan delivers tiger spice preferences as confident fact — 'tigers love pepper, they hate cinnamon' — with no possible source for this knowledge
jokes.explanation: One of the great Alan lines. The confidence with which he delivers completely unverifiable tiger-flavor-preference information — delivered as though it's common knowledge — is peak Alan. The specificity of the cinnamon detail is perfect: it's not just 'tigers like meat' but a specific spice hierarchy. 'They hate cinnamon' in particular is delivered with genuine conviction. Approaches the calibration anchor: extremely quotable, character-perfect, and a nearly perfect economy of words.

jokes.text: 'I jammed 5 roofies in there. Just go in there and throw it to him.'
jokes.setup: Stu is nervous about approaching the tiger with the drugged steak
jokes.punchline: Alan casually mentions he's already overloaded the steak with roofies — the same drug he already used on his friends — and encourages a nonchalant approach to a live tiger
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the roofie confession — Alan has already used this drug on his friends and has apparently been carrying a supply. 'I jammed 5 roofies in there' said as casual problem-solving is a great continuation of his character logic.

jokes.text: Alan begins singing an improvised song about the tiger set to a lullaby rhythm: 'What do tigers dream of when they take a little tiger snooze...'
jokes.setup: They are waiting for the tiger to fall asleep after Stu delivered the drugged steak
jokes.punchline: Alan begins an earnest, tender improvised song about tiger dreams, including references to Halle Berry as Catwoman and getting the tiger 'back to Tyson and your cozy tiger bed'
jokes.explanation: One of the best sustained Alan moments in the film. The song is both absurd and oddly sincere — Alan genuinely seems to be comforting the tiger. 'Halle Berry in her Catwoman suit' is a perfect specific detail that reveals Alan's inner world. 'Cozy tiger bed' is disarmingly sweet. The escalation from lullaby to 'if he's been murdered by crystal meth tweakers, well then we're shit out of luck' is a tonal whiplash that is structurally brilliant. Very high character integration — no one else in the film could sing this song.

jokes.text: 'But if he's been murdered by crystal meth tweakers... well then we're shit out of luck.'
jokes.setup: Alan's tiger lullaby is building to an optimistic conclusion about finding Doug
jokes.punchline: The lullaby pivots abruptly to a crystal meth murder scenario with a defeated shrug — 'we're shit out of luck' — before returning to the song
jokes.explanation: The tonal pivot from lullaby to murder scenario is structurally audacious and lands perfectly. The measured cadence of 'well then we're shit out of luck' — said in the same rhythmic voice as the rest of the song — creates a beautiful incongruity. It's also a callback to Stu's earlier meth-head theory, now adopted by Alan in song form.

jokes.text: During the tiger transport, someone in the front seat accidentally elbows the tiger's nose
jokes.setup: They are transporting the drugged tiger in the backseat of their car — an inherently absurd situation
jokes.punchline: 'Watch it. That's his nose.' — the mundane complaint about jostling a sleeping tiger as though it's an inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Decent beat — the normalization of tiger transport ('watch it, that's his nose') treats an impossible situation as ordinary, which is a consistent comic mechanism throughout this sequence. Functional humor.

jokes.text: Alan, roofied and drifting, asks 'Hey guys, when's the next Halley's Comet?' and after learning it's 60 years away, frets about missing it
jokes.setup: Alan is apparently having a drug reaction and starts asking non-sequitur questions during the tiger drive
jokes.punchline: 'I want to make sure I'll never ever miss out on Halley's Comet' — Alan's deeply personal fear about a 60-year astronomical event while seated next to a sleeping tiger
jokes.explanation: Classic Alan non-sequitur — the drug-addled mind going to Halley's Comet in a moment of tiger-related tension. The genuine emotional weight Alan gives to comet-anxiety is funny. 'I wanna make sure I'll never ever miss out' is the kind of sincere absurdity Alan excels at.

jokes.text: The tiger wakes up in the backseat and claws Phil
jokes.setup: They've been driving the supposedly sedated tiger back to Tyson's; Alan's Halley's Comet monologue has been a distraction
jokes.punchline: The tiger wakes up and mauls Phil's arm — the inevitable consequence of their absurd plan playing out
jokes.explanation: Effective physical escalation — the tiger waking up is the promised peril finally delivering. High impact in theaters due to shock value. Less strong on craft as it's a fairly predictable consequence of the setup.

jokes.text: 'Get your fuckin' hand back in there. You're steering the car.' / 'I'm too nervous.' / 'Alan, we need you, buddy. It's your time to shine.'
jokes.setup: Phil has been clawed and can no longer steer; they need Alan to take the wheel while a tiger is loose in the backseat
jokes.punchline: 'It's your time to shine' — Alan is drafted as emergency driver in a car with an awake tiger, framed as a heroic moment
jokes.explanation: 'It's your time to shine' as applied to a terrified Alan being coaxed into driving with a live tiger is a good framing joke. The escalation of their situation — from bad to catastrophically worse — works with momentum.

jokes.text: 'That's me. I'm on TV. I've never been on TV before.' (while watching security footage of them committing crimes)
jokes.setup: Tyson's team shows them security footage that reveals what they did the night before — including crimes
jokes.punchline: Alan's reaction to appearing in incriminating security footage is pure excitement at being on TV for the first time
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The discrepancy between Alan's reaction (TV celebrity excitement) and the appropriate reaction (horror at evidence of crimes) is perfectly absurd. 'I've never been on TV before' said with genuine wonder about security footage is quotable and completely Alan. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'Maybe I... should I wait outside?' / 'I think that's a good idea.' / 'Don't touch anything out there either. He's not our good... we don't know him that well.'
jokes.setup: Alan keeps interjecting excitedly while they're trying to watch the security footage in the presence of Tyson's intimidating associates
jokes.punchline: Phil agrees Alan should wait outside, then immediately adds 'we don't know him that well' — distancing themselves from Alan in front of Tyson's crew
jokes.explanation: 'We don't know him that well' is a great disavowal joke — Phil publicly cutting Alan loose in front of strangers is funny and character-consistent (Phil is the most self-interested of the group). The phrasing 'He's not our good...' trailing off before the correction adds texture.

jokes.text: 'By the way, man, where did you get that cop car from?' / 'We stole it from these dumbass cops.' / 'Nice. High five.'
jokes.setup: Tyson's associate asks about the cop car
jokes.punchline: Phil takes a high five from Tyson's associate for stealing a cop car — casually bonding with criminals over crimes they can't remember committing
jokes.explanation: Fun social-dynamics joke — Phil instinctively high-fiving a criminal for a crime he doesn't remember committing reveals something about Phil's character. The 'nice' approval from Tyson's associate is unexpected and funny.

jokes.text: 'I have to say, I've never seen a more beautiful, elegant, regal creature.' / 'Check it out, Stu. Fuck this tiger.' (security footage reveals the guys urinating on/near the tiger)
jokes.setup: Phil has just been watching the tiger with awe, calling it beautiful and regal
jokes.punchline: The security footage reveals that drunk-Phil's past behavior toward the same tiger was 'fuck this tiger' — the complete inversion of his current reverence
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke built on contrast. Phil's formal appreciation ('beautiful, elegant, regal') immediately followed by his past self's raw hostility ('fuck this tiger') is a perfect double-beat. The security footage as a callback mechanism is well-used here. 'Fuck this tiger' has become one of the film's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: 'Who does shit like that, man?' / 'Someone who has a lot of issues obviously.' / 'I'm a sick man.'
jokes.setup: Security footage shows one of them doing something outrageous with/to the tiger
jokes.punchline: Alan calmly self-diagnoses: 'I'm a sick man' — accepting the assessment without protest
jokes.explanation: Alan's serene self-acceptance of being a sick man is excellent character comedy. The lack of defensiveness is funnier than protest would be.

jokes.text: 'I'm a sick man.'
jokes.setup: They are watching security footage of themselves doing something awful to or near the tiger
jokes.punchline: Stu's quiet, resigned self-diagnosis — 'I'm a sick man' — delivered as genuine horror at his own past behavior
jokes.explanation: Three words that land as a perfect button to the security footage revelation. 'I'm a sick man' said with quiet devastation is a great Stu character beat — his periodic moments of genuine self-awareness are funnier than his rants.

jokes.text: 'We're so sorry we stole your tiger.' / 'Don't worry about it. Like you said, we all do dumb shit when we're fucked up.' / 'I did say that.'
jokes.setup: Phil is apologizing to Tyson for stealing his tiger
jokes.punchline: Tyson quotes Phil's earlier line back at him as forgiveness; Phil confirms he did say that — with a beat of amused self-recognition
jokes.explanation: Solid callback. Tyson using Phil's own philosophical shrug to forgive the tiger theft is satisfying and characterizes Tyson as more self-aware than expected. 'I did say that' as Phil's quiet acknowledgment is a nice button.

jokes.text: 'Everyone says Mike Tyson is a badass, but I think he's kind of a sweetheart.' / 'I think he's mean.'
jokes.setup: They're leaving Tyson's property; Alan is reflecting on the experience
jokes.punchline: Alan, who was punched in the face by Tyson and then said he 'still has it,' now reassesses him as a sweetheart; Stu, who was not punched, flatly disagrees
jokes.explanation: Good character-divergence joke. Alan adopting a paternal affection for the man who punched him is very Alan — his view of human relationships is upside-down. Stu's flat correction from outside the experience is a perfect contrast beat.

jokes.text: 'We don't need to tell her everything. We can leave out the stuff about me marrying a hooker.'
jokes.setup: Phil suggests they call Tracy (the groom's fiancée) and be completely honest
jokes.punchline: Stu immediately identifies the one piece of information to suppress — his accidental marriage — with no regard for the other dozens of insane things that happened
jokes.explanation: Good character beat that reveals Stu's self-serving priorities. His immediate filtering of the most personally embarrassing info — while apparently accepting that Mike Tyson, stolen cars, and a tiger are fine to share — is funny. The word 'hooker' is itself a mild callback to his earlier 'whore' statement.

jokes.text: They are rear-ended by Mr. Chow's car at a stop — 'Oh, Jesus.' / 'Oh, my god.'
jokes.setup: They're having a relatively calm conversation about calling Tracy
jokes.punchline: Mr. Chow reappears and rams their car — the kidnapping plot begins with a sudden automotive attack
jokes.explanation: Primarily a plot beat and callback to Mr. Chow. The comedic value is in the sudden recurrence of the same threat. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: 'I know that guy. That's the guy from the trunk.'
jokes.setup: A car rams into them; a man gets out
jokes.punchline: Alan recognizes the man from the trunk — Mr. Chow — connecting the two chaotic sequences while remaining perfectly calm about being rammed
jokes.explanation: Functional callback recognition beat. Alan's matter-of-fact identification of the man who attacked them ('that's the guy from the trunk') is mildly funny but mostly a plot connector.

jokes.text: 'I want my purse back, assholes.' / 'Your purse?' / 'That's not a purse, it's a satchel.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Chow confronts them about stealing his purse
jokes.punchline: Alan insists it's a 'satchel' — defending the semantic honor of a bag Mr. Chow just called a purse, while holding said bag hostage
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Alan's immediate deflection to nomenclature defense ('it's a satchel') is very consistent with his character's sideways logic. It also works as a mild Indiana Jones reference. Quotable and character-integrated.

jokes.text: 'Mine had 80 thousand dollars inside.' / 'And this one? Nothing.' / 'Hey, there's skittles in there.'
jokes.setup: Chow establishes his purse had $80K; they apparently have a different bag with nothing valuable
jokes.punchline: Alan finds Skittles in the bag and reports this discovery with equal gravity to Chow's $80K revelation
jokes.explanation: Excellent small beat. 'Hey, there's Skittles in there' delivered with the same tone as a significant discovery perfectly captures Alan's value system. It also implies Alan may have already swapped the bags and kept the Skittles as the prize. Great economy — four words land big.

jokes.text: 'Don't let the beard fool you. He's a child.' / 'He's funny because he's fat.'
jokes.setup: Chow is frustrated with Alan's Skittles comment; Phil tries to contextualize Alan
jokes.punchline: Chow's assessment — 'he's funny because he's fat' — is a bizarrely reductive meta-commentary on Zach Galifianakis himself, delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: One of the most meta lines in the film — Chow's 'he's funny because he's fat' is a straight-faced commentary on Galifianakis's screen persona that works on multiple levels. Phil's setup ('he's a child') is excellent too. Slightly uncomfortable self-referential edge makes it memorable.

jokes.text: 'He starts screaming like crazy, and throw me in trunk.' (Chow explains that drunk-Alan kidnapped him as a 'lucky charm')
jokes.setup: Chow explains why he was in their trunk
jokes.punchline: Drunk-Alan apparently kidnapped a stranger from a craps table because he thought the man was his lucky charm, then threw him in the trunk screaming
jokes.explanation: Excellent retroactive reveal comedy — the explanation of past-Alan's behavior (kidnapping a lucky charm) is both completely insane and entirely consistent with Alan's character. 'Lucky charm' as a kidnapping motivation is one of the best Alan-behavior explanations in the film.

jokes.text: 'You said he was your lucky charm. And you wanted to take him home with you.' / 'Lucky charm.' / 'That's just funny.'
jokes.setup: Chow has just explained Alan kidnapped him as a lucky charm
jokes.punchline: Phil's reaction — a beat, then 'that's just funny' — delivered with the amusement of a man who is beginning to accept Alan's absurdity
jokes.explanation: Phil's 'that's just funny' is a reaction beat that works because of his delivery — it's the laugh of a man who has given up trying to make sense of Alan. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: 'You can't have our friend. Kidnapper!'
jokes.setup: Chow is driving away with Doug; the men are trying to stop him
jokes.punchline: Alan's protest — 'Kidnapper!' shouted as though it's a legal citation — is the most ineffectual response possible to a man who is actively kidnapping someone
jokes.explanation: Alan's formal legal accusation directed at a retreating criminal is a good character beat — he lives in a world where naming a thing should stop it. The exclamation mark delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: 'Run me over.' — Chow offers this as an alternative to the hostage exchange
jokes.setup: They're negotiating with Chow over the hostage
jokes.punchline: Chow genuinely invites being run over as a valid negotiating option — with the flat confidence of a man who has considered it
jokes.explanation: 'Run me over' is two words and yet completely unhinged. It's delivered with Chow's characteristic bravado — he genuinely means it as an option. Perfect economy and very quotable. The character specificity is high; this is entirely Mr. Chow's brand of insane confidence.

jokes.text: 'Bring money to Big Rock in Mojave Desert at dawn. Toodle-loo, mothafucka.'
jokes.setup: Chow issues a ransom ultimatum for Doug
jokes.punchline: 'Toodle-loo, mothafucka' — the most extreme tonal whiplash possible to close a ransom demand
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a perfect character-defining moment for Mr. Chow. 'Toodle-loo' is the most genteel, British-nanny farewell imaginable; 'mothafucka' is the most aggressive possible closer. The collision of these two registers is delightful. It's also totally character-consistent — Chow is defined by tonal unpredictability. Economy is flawless: five words, two entirely incompatible registers, maximum impact.

jokes.text: 'At least take the bag off his head.'
jokes.setup: Chow has driven away with Doug; everyone is in shock
jokes.punchline: Alan's last-resort reasonable request — after failing to prevent the kidnapping, he asks only that they remove the bag from Doug's head — delivered with no sense of irony
jokes.explanation: Excellent deflation joke. After the chaos of the encounter, Alan's only remaining ask — the most basic possible comfort request for a kidnap victim — is oddly touching and funny. The sincerity is what makes it work: Alan genuinely thinks this is a reasonable ask.

jokes.text: 'You're already married. So we're good there.' / 'Besides, not for Melissa. She's the worst. Doug told me she had sex with a pilot.' / 'It was a bartender on a cruise. What is wrong with you people.'
jokes.setup: Stu says he was going to use his savings for the wedding
jokes.punchline: Phil points out Stu is already married (to the stripper), then casually mentions Melissa's infidelity; Stu corrects the specific infidelity details, revealing he already knew and has been cataloguing them
jokes.explanation: Good multi-layer joke. Phil's casual mention of Melissa cheating is a bomb; Stu's correction of the details ('it was a bartender on a cruise') reveals he has been aware and has been keeping specific records of her infidelity — which explains his rage throughout the film. 'What is wrong with you people' as his response to them knowing is a great button.

jokes.text: 'Besides, not for Melissa. She's the worst.' / 'Doug told me she had sex with a pilot or something like that.' / 'It was a bartender on a cruise. What is wrong with you people.'
jokes.setup: Phil dismisses Melissa while they discuss Stu's money; Alan has secondhand gossip about Melissa
jokes.punchline: Alan has the gossip wrong — 'pilot' vs. 'bartender on a cruise' — and Stu's correction reveals he knows the specific details of his fiancée's infidelity intimately
jokes.explanation: Stu's correction reveals the most damning detail — he has the exact specifics memorized ('bartender on a cruise'), which shows how badly this relationship is compromised. 'What is wrong with you people' as his only response to being cheated on is brilliantly sad. Alan getting the gossip wrong adds a layer.

jokes.text: 'Alan, did you just eat sofa pizza?'
jokes.setup: They are discussing their dire situation with no money and a kidnapped friend
jokes.punchline: Alan has apparently been eating pizza off the sofa this entire time — 'sofa pizza' as a concept is both disgusting and completely Alan
jokes.explanation: Very funny visual gag delivered through dialogue. 'Sofa pizza' as a noun — implying Alan has been casually eating pizza that was on or under the sofa in a hotel they trashed — is disgusting and perfect for his character. Phil's tone is not angry, just wearily incredulous. High character integration: sofa pizza is exactly what Alan would do.

jokes.text: Shut up, Vincent.
jokes.setup: The group is at a blackjack table trying to win big; someone (presumably a stranger named Vincent) is offering unsolicited commentary on their play.
jokes.punchline: Phil's curt dismissal — 'Shut up, Vincent' — is delivered as if he's known this annoying man his whole life, despite just sitting down.
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat establishing Phil's no-nonsense attitude. The specificity of the name 'Vincent' — delivered as if it's a long-standing annoyance — earns a mild laugh. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I don't even know you. But I'm gonna tell you, that's dumb.
jokes.setup: Alan splits a pair of 5s — a terrible blackjack move. A stranger at the table reacts.
jokes.punchline: The stranger prefaces his critique with 'I don't even know you' — which somehow makes the judgment feel even more damning.
jokes.explanation: The 'I don't even know you, but...' structure is a recognizable comedic frame that works here because it underlines Alan's idiocy. Competent and funny but not remarkable.

jokes.text: I'm such a klutz. I get so nervous when I gamble. I'm so silly.
characters: Jade (woman at blackjack table, working as a distraction)
jokes.setup: The group is running a casino con — they need a distraction to draw attention from Alan's card-counting. A woman creates a commotion by 'accidentally' knocking something over.
jokes.punchline: Her over-the-top, performed helplessness ('I'm so silly!') is transparently fake, which is the joke — she's doing a bad actress job of a scripted distraction.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic beat in the casino con sequence. The layered irony — she's performing helplessness badly on purpose — works, but it's a familiar trope. Gets a mild chuckle.

jokes.text: Sorry. She's had a little too much drink. Thanks, buddy. That's for you.
jokes.setup: The woman's 'accident' has drawn the pit boss away. Phil/Stu smoothly tips the security guard while casually excusing the fake stumble.
jokes.punchline: The breezy, 'that's for you' tip — as if this is all perfectly normal — underscores the casual criminality of the whole operation.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh beat — more plot glue than comedy. The casual bribery is mildly amusing but not a crafted joke.

jokes.text: We should come back next week. Take the whole city down. I'm free next week. Or we could just focus on getting Doug back right now.
jokes.setup: The group has just won $82,400 counting cards. Exhilaration takes over and they start fantasizing about coming back.
jokes.punchline: Stu is the only one who remembers they are supposed to be rescuing their kidnapped friend — the others have completely forgotten the mission in their excitement.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Phil and Alan's moral drift is funny, and Stu's voice-of-reason role is well-established. The pivot from heist triumph to 'wait, we have a kidnapped friend' is a solid structural joke.

jokes.text: Next week is no good for me. The Jonas Brothers are in town. But any week after that, it's totally fine.
jokes.setup: Everyone is riding high on the casino win; Phil suggests coming back next week to 'take the city down.'
jokes.punchline: Alan declines because the Jonas Brothers are in town — a completely unexpected, childlike non sequitur that reveals his priorities entirely.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Alan character joke. The Jonas Brothers reference is perfectly incongruous in a scene of hard-boiled casino con triumph — only Alan would have this priority. The follow-up 'but any week after that, it's totally fine' extends the absurdity and deepens the laugh. High character integration: this could only be Alan.

jokes.text: And we're the three best friends that anybody could have. We're the three best friends that anyone can have.
jokes.setup: Earlier in the film Alan sang this song sincerely; the group is now euphoric after the casino win.
jokes.punchline: The song returns at peak absurdity — grown men singing a children's-style friendship anthem while fleeing a casino con — and their earnestness makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Callback to one of the film's signature bits. The song works here because the joy is genuine and earned — they won — but the song itself remains ridiculous. High quotability. Gains most of its power as a callback.

jokes.text: What signal? Flash your lights. What's on? The deal. Of course it's on. We just drove 30 miles into the desert. He knows it's on.
jokes.setup: The group has driven to a desert handoff to exchange money for Doug. Phil is told to 'give the signal.'
jokes.punchline: The 'signal' was apparently never agreed upon, and when pressed, Phil's logic ('we drove 30 miles, he knows it's on') is both hilarious and completely sound.
jokes.explanation: Good banter. Phil's frustrated logic is relatable and funny. The setup/payoff works, though it's a fairly standard 'plan goes wrong' comedy beat.

jokes.text: Funny. The fat guy fall on face.
jokes.setup: During the tense desert money exchange, Alan presumably trips and falls face-first.
jokes.punchline: Mr. Chow, the villain, cannot help but narrate Alan's physical pratfall with gleeful mockery in his broken English.
jokes.explanation: Mr. Chow's broken-English commentary on Alan's pratfall is both a visual gag and a character comedy beat. 'The fat guy fall on face' is oddly poetic in its bluntness and economy. High quotability; Chow's voice is distinctive and memorable.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. First of all, good morning. We didn't catch your name last night.
jokes.setup: Mr. Chow has just said 'give me the money or I shoot you all.' This is a life-or-death situation.
jokes.punchline: Stu responds with the pleasantries of a business meeting — 'good morning,' 'we didn't catch your name' — as if the guns aren't there.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Stu character moment. His conflict-averse, overly polite nature manifests at the worst possible time. The deflation of a gun-threat with 'good morning' is well-executed and character-specific. Strong craft.

jokes.text: Of course, Stu. That is cool.
jokes.setup: Stu has politely asked to verify Doug is okay before handing over the ransom money.
jokes.punchline: The crime lord sincerely confirms 'That is cool' — slipping into casual American slang during a hostage exchange — a jarring register shift that lands perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Ken Jeong's Chow is a comedic force and this quick line shows why — the villainous register breaking into 'That is cool' is funny precisely because it matches Stu's politeness in kind, escalating the absurdity of the whole exchange.

jokes.text: Ta-da. Is this some kind of a joke? Who the hell is this? That is not Doug.
jokes.setup: $80,000 has changed hands in a desert hostage exchange. Mr. Chow theatrically reveals 'Doug.'
jokes.punchline: The 'Doug' revealed is a Black man — not their friend at all. Chow had the wrong hostage the entire time.
jokes.explanation: Major comedic reversal — the film's central tension (find Doug) is both resolved and re-broken in a single beat. 'Ta-da' from Chow is a perfect setup for the reveal. The structure is tight: payment, flourish, reveal, reaction. High impact because the audience has been building toward this moment for the whole film.

jokes.text: I told you you had the wrong guy, little boy.
jokes.setup: The wrong-Doug reveal has just happened. Everyone is stunned.
jokes.punchline: The wrongly-kidnapped man calmly tells Mr. Chow 'I told you you had the wrong guy, little boy' — implying he said this during captivity and was ignored, and the condescending 'little boy' to a crime lord is an unexpected power move.
jokes.explanation: 'Little boy' directed at the volatile Mr. Chow is a surprising power play from a man who was just held hostage. The implication that he tried to explain the mistake and was ignored is a funny bit of world-building delivered in one line.

jokes.text: Damn, Alan. What the fuck you got me into? You know him? Yeah. This is the guy that sell me the bad drugs. How you doin'?
jokes.setup: Black Doug is furious about being kidnapped. He turns on Alan.
jokes.punchline: He recognizes Alan as a customer who bought bad drugs from his dealer — and immediately the whole thing becomes a small-world drug deal situation, with Alan cheerily asking 'How you doin'?'
jokes.explanation: Good callback that connects the drug subplot with the wrong-Doug reveal. Alan's breezy 'How you doin'?' while chaos erupts around him is a strong character beat. Escalation of the comedic situation.

jokes.text: Who gives a shit! Where is Doug? I am Doug. His name's Doug too. Classic mixed up.
jokes.setup: The argument about drugs and kidnapping is derailing; Phil tries to refocus on finding their Doug.
jokes.punchline: The wrong Doug's name is also Doug. Alan's delighted 'Classic mixed up' treats a catastrophe as a fun coincidence.
jokes.explanation: 'Classic mixed up' is a gem — Alan cheerfully diagnoses a catastrophic failure as a cute oopsie. High character integration, high quotability. His tone of delighted fascination rather than horror is the whole joke.

jokes.text: No. Come on, man. I'll be your Doug.
jokes.setup: The group demands their money back and want to give Black Doug back to Chow.
jokes.punchline: Black Doug, faced with returning to captivity with Chow, sincerely offers to serve as a substitute Doug for the wedding — 'I'll be your Doug.'
jokes.explanation: 'I'll be your Doug' is a funny, desperate bid — the implicit comparison of returning to Chow versus being an impostor groom lands well. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Right after you suck on this little Chinese nuts. Oh, that's nasty. How that sound? So long, gay boys.
jokes.setup: Mr. Chow is taking Black Doug back and declaring victory over the group.
jokes.punchline: His departing insults — 'suck on this little Chinese nuts' and 'So long, gay boys' — are delivered with such unhinged gusto that his villainy becomes pure absurdist comedy.
jokes.explanation: Chow's exit is pure, deranged character comedy. His complete lack of filter and the triumphant delivery of crude insults is funny because it's so at odds with the high-stakes situation. High quotability and character integration. The humor is in the character's unhinged energy rather than clever construction.

jokes.text: God, damn it! Gosh, darn it! Shit! Shoot!
jokes.setup: The plan has completely failed — $80,000 gone, still no Doug.
jokes.punchline: Phil says 'God damn it,' Alan echoes with 'Gosh darn it'; Phil says 'Shit,' Alan says 'Shoot.' Alan's compulsive sanitizing of profanity during a catastrophe reveals his oddly innocent core.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best character jokes. The parallel structure — real profanity / sanitized echo — is tight and reveals something true about Alan: for all his drug-taking and chaos-creating, he won't swear. 'Gosh darn it' and 'Shoot' in this context are perfectly absurd. High character integration, excellent economy, very quotable.

jokes.text: Thanks for the lift back to town. [reaction beat — the group driving back with the man who was just held hostage, perfectly normal]
jokes.setup: After the total failure of the ransom exchange, the group is driving back to Las Vegas.
jokes.punchline: Black Doug is apparently in the car, hitching a ride back to town — the casual normalization of this bizarre situation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational beat — the fact that everyone has just accepted this stranger into their car after a botched ransom exchange is funny in a low-key way. Not a big laugh but adds texture.

jokes.text: Black Doug: 'We were shooting craps. You don't remember?' The trio: 'No. We don't remember.'
jokes.setup: Black Doug is filling them in on the night's events they can't recall
jokes.punchline: Their total amnesia is played as a straight fact — 'No. We don't remember. Because some dick drug dealer sold him roofilin and told him it was ecstasy' — which reframes the entire situation with perfect deadpan indignation
jokes.explanation: Functional reminder of the central premise. Gets a small laugh from the ongoing absurdity but doesn't generate new comedy — it's expository.

jokes.text: Roofilin. There you go with that word, Roofilin. What the hell is a Roofilin?
jokes.setup: Stu says 'roofilin' — a mispronunciation of 'roofies' (Rohypnol) — and Black Doug fixates on it.
jokes.punchline: His genuine bafflement at 'Roofilin' — as a drug dealer adjacent to the scene — becomes a running joke about Alan/Stu's bizarre vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: The 'roofilin' gag is a callback that gains new life here because an actual drug-world figure is baffled by it. The logic — why would someone in the drug trade not know the word? — is funny and the outrage is proportional.

jokes.text: Wow. You are the world's shittiest drug dealer.
jokes.setup: The drug dealer has just admitted he accidentally gave Alan roofies instead of ecstasy, apparently by mixing up his bags.
jokes.punchline: Phil's flat, comprehensive summation — 'world's shittiest drug dealer' — is perfect economy.
jokes.explanation: 'World's shittiest drug dealer' is a clean, perfectly constructed insult — it summarizes the entire subplot (accidental roofie-ing, inadvertent kidnapping, $80K lost) in four words. Good economy.

jokes.text: Why do you even call 'em roofies? Why not floories? Cuz when you take 'em, you're more likely to end up on the floor than the roof.
jokes.setup: Black Doug is philosophizing about drug names while everyone else is in crisis mode.
jokes.punchline: His completely irrelevant but internally logical argument for renaming roofies 'floories' is perfectly absurd — a drug dealer doing amateur etymology while the group spirals.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The comedic logic is internally consistent — you DO end up on the floor, not the roof — which makes the absurdity feel earned. The timing (everyone is in crisis, he's doing wordplay) is pitch-perfect. 'Floories' is a genuinely funny neologism. High quotability and originality.

jokes.text: What about groundies? That's a good new name for 'em.
jokes.setup: Black Doug has just proposed 'floories' as a better name for roofies.
jokes.punchline: Stu — the voice of reason — immediately engages with the drug-renaming game and offers 'groundies,' completely forgetting the crisis.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the naming game — from 'floories' to 'groundies' — is funny because Stu, the responsible one, is now fully participating. The character betrayal is the joke. 'Groundies' is also just a funny word.

jokes.text: What about groundies. That's a good new name for'em.
jokes.setup: Black Doug has proposed 'floories' as a better name for roofies; Alan engages with this logic completely sincerely.
jokes.punchline: Alan's earnest counter-proposal of 'groundies' — taking the same logic one step further with equal seriousness — shows his total buy-in to irrelevant tangents.
jokes.explanation: Alan's sincerity is what makes this work. He's not making fun of the conversation — he's genuinely participating and improving on it. 'Groundies' is a funny word. The deadpan follow-up 'That's a good new name for em' sells it as Alan's considered opinion.

jokes.text: Or how bout rapies?
jokes.setup: Stu has proposed 'groundies' in the drug-renaming game.
jokes.punchline: Alan's contribution — 'rapies' — escalates the game into genuinely dark territory. The horrified reaction from the group and the sudden silence signals the line has been crossed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark escalation. Alan, in complete innocence, arrives at the logical endpoint of the naming game — a drug called 'rapies' — without registering the horror of it. His obliviousness is the character's defining trait and it's never cleaner than here. The comedic peak of the naming sequence. High character integration (only Alan), excellent economy (one word), and the stunned reaction amplifies the impact.

jokes.text: Phil calling Tracy with a cover story — 'Nothing. Don't listen to Phil. He's completely out of his mind. He's probably still drunk from last night. Where's Doug? He is paying the bill. We just had a delicious brunch.'
jokes.setup: Phil has started to tell Tracy the truth about their situation. Stu grabs the phone.
jokes.punchline: Stu's frantic pivot to a completely fabricated 'delicious brunch' story — building an elaborate lie in real time — is hilarious because of how specific and desperate 'delicious brunch' is as a detail.
jokes.explanation: Good Stu character beat — his panic-improvised 'delicious brunch' is funny because it's simultaneously too specific (why describe the brunch at all?) and completely inadequate cover for the situation. Character-specific and structurally sound.

jokes.text: Do you remember when we saw Doug's mattress impaled on that statue? Yeah, it's because we threw it out the window. No, it's impossible. You can't open windows in Vegas hotels.
jokes.setup: Stu is working backward through the evidence to figure out where Doug is.
jokes.punchline: Phil says 'we threw it out the window,' Alan correctly notes 'you can't open windows in Vegas hotels' — which means they threw it out MORE dramatically than through a window, implying something insane happened.
jokes.explanation: Good logical comedy — the Vegas hotel window fact is correct and its implication (they broke the window with a mattress, or did something more extreme) escalates the mystery of the night. Solid structural joke.

jokes.text: Holy shit. How did you figure that out? Doug made me realize it. Doug? Not our Doug. Black Doug. Hey, easy with that shit.
jokes.setup: Stu has deduced Doug is on the roof. Phil asks how. Stu credits 'Doug.'
jokes.punchline: The 'which Doug?' confusion plays out again, and when Stu says 'Black Doug,' Black Doug objects to the label — 'Hey, easy with that shit.'
jokes.explanation: The two-Dougs running gag with Black Doug's objection to the label is a good extension of the bit. His indignation ('easy with that shit') is well-delivered and fair — the audience has been laughing at his expense and his pushback lands.

jokes.text: It's like that time in summer camp. Remember when we moved his sleeping bag out in the jetty in the lake? Which was hilarious. It's not so funny now, though, cuz we forgot where we put him.
jokes.setup: They've realized they put Doug on the roof as a prank and forgot about him.
jokes.punchline: The summer camp callback — presented as whimsical nostalgia — is immediately deflated: 'It's not so funny now though because we forgot where we put him.'
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'which was hilarious' to 'it's not so funny now because we forgot where we put him' is a decent joke structure. The retrospective framing of a catastrophe as a classic prank-gone-wrong is functional comedy.

jokes.text: You guys are fuckin' retarded. You know that?
jokes.setup: The group has just explained they put their friend on a roof as a prank and forgot about him for two days.
jokes.punchline: Black Doug's incredulous summary captures the audience's feeling perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Functional audience-surrogate reaction — Black Doug voices what the audience is thinking. But it's a lazy comedic device (character says the obvious) with no real craft. Gets a chuckle from recognition, not construction.

jokes.text: You look good. You got some color. I'm jealous.
jokes.setup: Doug has been found on the roof — severely sunburned, dehydrated, furious. He's clearly been there for two days.
jokes.punchline: Phil's response to Doug's obvious distress is to compliment his tan — 'You got some color. I'm jealous.' — delivered completely straight.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. Phil's sociopathic social skills shine: faced with a catastrophe of his own making, he leads with a compliment about Doug's tan. 'I'm jealous' is the kicker that makes it exceptional — it's not just obliviousness, it's Phil genuinely coveting the sunburn. Excellent economy and character integration. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I'm getting married today. Yes, Doug, that's why you need to focus and do everything we say. Because frankly you're wasting a little bit of time right now.
jokes.setup: Doug is furious and disoriented after two days on a roof.
jokes.punchline: Phil tells the sunburned, abandoned groom that HE is the one wasting time — the reversal of guilt is Phil at his most casually monstrous.
jokes.explanation: 'You're wasting a little bit of time right now' is a beautiful example of Phil's character — he abandoned his friend on a roof and is now annoyed at the friend for being upset. The measured, slightly exasperated delivery ('frankly') elevates it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: It's okay. It's not your fault, Doug. Don't touch me. Shut up. All of you shut up.
jokes.setup: Doug is furious and burning. Alan tries to comfort him.
jokes.punchline: Doug's vicious rejection of Alan's comfort — 'Don't touch me. Shut up. All of you shut up.' — after Alan's sweetly sincere 'It's not your fault' is a good cringe beat.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat. Doug's rejection of Alan's sincere sweetness is relatable — Alan is the reason he's here — but the joke is fairly predictable.

jokes.text: Is he missing a tooth? Yeah.
jokes.setup: Everyone is scrambling to leave. Doug notices Stu for the first time.
jokes.punchline: The brief, matter-of-fact exchange — 'Is he missing a tooth?' / 'Yeah' — treats the tooth-pulling revelation as completely unremarkable in the larger chaos.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire Stu tooth subplot is acknowledged in two words. The deadpan acceptance ('Yeah') as an answer to 'is he missing a tooth?' is funny because it closes the question immediately. The rewatch bonus is high because viewers knowing the full story enjoy the compression.

jokes.text: Phil: 'We will leave without you' — said to Doug (the man they just rescued and whose wedding they need to attend) while he takes a moment
jokes.setup: Doug asks for 'just one second' — he's been abandoned on a roof for two days and is recovering
jokes.punchline: Phil threatens to leave Doug AGAIN, with zero self-awareness, immediately after rescuing him
jokes.explanation: Phil threatening to leave the guy they just found, right after abandoning him for two days, is a great dark-irony beat. 'We will leave without you' as a genuine threat from his rescuers is deliciously cruel. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Thank you. I can't believe I gave my grandmother's holocaust ring to someone I just met. What was I thinking? You were really fucked up. Clearly.
jokes.setup: Stu is returning Jade's ring (which he used to propose during their blackout night).
jokes.punchline: The ring is revealed to be a Holocaust-survivor grandmother's ring — the specificity of this detail escalates from 'regrettable impulse' to 'actual family heirloom horror.' Stu's 'You were really fucked up' / 'Clearly' capper is a good dry exchange.
jokes.explanation: The Holocaust ring detail is a great dark escalation — it makes Jade's poor judgment maximally specific and consequential. The 'You were really fucked up' / 'Clearly' capper is deadpan and efficient. The specificity is what makes this more than a generic 'bad night' joke.

jokes.text: You did pull out your own tooth. I pulled out my tooth? Why did I pull out my own tooth? Alan bet you you weren't a good enough dentist to pull out your own tooth. Okay, of course he did.
jokes.setup: Stu is asking Jade to fill in the gaps of the night.
jokes.punchline: The explanation for Stu's missing tooth — Alan bet him he wasn't a good enough dentist to do it himself — is both perfectly in character for Alan and deeply horrifying as dental self-surgery.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The explanation for the tooth is perfectly Alan: he framed it as a competency challenge ('you weren't a good enough dentist'). Stu's resigned 'Okay, of course he did' is the ideal reaction — he's not even surprised anymore. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jade: 'You did pull out your own tooth.' Stu: 'I pulled out my own tooth?' — stunned. 'Why did I pull out my own tooth?' Alan: 'Because I bet you you weren't a good enough dentist to pull out your own tooth.'
jokes.setup: Stu has been walking around toothless for the whole film; the reason has never been revealed
jokes.punchline: Alan bet him he couldn't do it — using Stu's professional pride as a dentist against him in the most self-destructive possible wager
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the film's longest running visual gag is excellent. The reveal is both surprising and inevitable — of course Alan bet him, and of COURSE it was framed as a professional competence challenge. The character integration score is near-maximum: only Alan would make this bet, only Stu (a dentist with a pride problem) would accept it, and the bet reveals something true about both characters. 'Because I bet you you weren't a good enough dentist to pull out your own tooth' is quotable, economical, and earns its laugh through 90 minutes of setup.

jokes.text: But you won. Yeah, clearly. That's victory right there.
jokes.setup: Stu has been told he bet Alan he could pull out his own tooth — and did.
jokes.punchline: Alan's earnest 'That's victory right there' about Stu's self-performed emergency dental surgery is the capper — Alan genuinely believes this was a triumph.
jokes.explanation: 'That's victory right there' is a great Alan line — his sincere pride in Stu's traumatic self-dentistry captures his entire worldview. 'Victory' is the precise wrong word deployed with total conviction. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: No. I gotta get it down first. [Alan forces the seat down before getting in the car; everyone yells at him]
jokes.setup: Everyone is screaming to leave immediately; every second counts. The seat needs to go down to fit people in.
jokes.punchline: Alan insists on being the one to get it down and presumably fumbles with it while everyone screams — his methodical approach to a micro-task during a macro-crisis is pure Alan.
jokes.explanation: Minor Alan character beat. His insistence on personally handling the seat while the wedding clock ticks is classic Alan prioritization. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: What are you doing next weekend? I don't know, working, why? Cuz I was thinking maybe I'll come back and take us to dinner or something. Really? Like a date? Yeah, like a date. Only the one that I hopefully remember.
jokes.setup: Stu is saying goodbye to Jade — his accidental wife — in a rush because they're late for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: He asks her on a real date, qualifies it with 'only the one that I hopefully remember' — a callback to the entire blackout premise that also reveals genuine feelings.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny simultaneously — the callback to the blackout ('only the one I hopefully remember') earns a laugh while also being genuinely charming. Good structural balance of comedy and heart. Stu's awkward romanticism in a crunch is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: At least the trip wasn't a total disaster. What makes you say that? When I woke up on the roof, I happened to find $80,000 worth of Bellagio chips in my pocket.
jokes.setup: Everyone is in the car, exhausted, having lost $80,000 and barely making it to the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Doug casually reveals he woke up with $80,000 in Bellagio chips — the money they just handed to Chow was apparently already won the night before by Doug.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — the $80,000 paid out was effectively replaced by the chips in Doug's pocket. The comedic irony that they paid $80k in cash and immediately got $80k back in chips is satisfying and structurally clean. The understatement 'at least the trip wasn't a total disaster' as a setup is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Hey, Victor! [a speeding car/motorbike narrowly misses someone — 'Wow, look out! Oh, shit!'] Thanks, Vic. Adios. Who the hell was that guy? That's my buddy.
jokes.setup: Alan signals his contact Victor to get them through traffic. Victor arrives in a blaze.
jokes.punchline: Victor nearly runs someone down, then speeds off; Alan cheerfully waves 'Adios' and when asked who that was, says simply 'That's my buddy' — as if this is a completely normal acquaintance.
jokes.explanation: Alan's social world is a constant source of comedy — he has 'buddies' who are apparently unhinged. 'That's my buddy' as a complete explanation for a near-vehicular-incident is a good Alan line. Functional character bit.

jokes.text: How's my hair? It's good. Is it cool like Phil's? It's classic Phil.
jokes.setup: They're arriving at the wedding venue. Alan wants to look good.
jokes.punchline: Alan's aspirational question — 'Is it cool like Phil's?' — reveals his admiration for Phil; 'It's classic Phil' is a deliberately ambiguous non-answer (is 'classic Phil' a good thing?).
jokes.explanation: Sweet Alan character beat — his reverence for Phil is a consistent thread. 'It's classic Phil' as a dodgy compliment/non-answer is mildly funny. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Sorry I'm late. Vegas.
jokes.setup: Doug arrives to his own wedding, sunburned, disheveled, almost late.
jokes.punchline: His entire explanation for a two-day absence and his condition is one word: 'Vegas.' It functions as a full confession and apology simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel on pure economy. 'Vegas.' as a complete explanation for all of the preceding 90 minutes of film is perfect.
