It's the best possible punchline to the entire movie's first act — it explains everything and nothing simultaneously. The delivery undercuts two days of chaos into one resigned syllable. Extremely quotable, perfectly economical.

jokes.text: 50 Cent's 'Candy Shop' plays at the wedding — 'I'll take you to the candy shop, I'll let you lick the lollipop...'
jokes.setup: A wedding ceremony or reception is underway with music.
jokes.punchline: The song playing is 50 Cent's explicitly sexual 'Candy Shop' — an absurd and inappropriate choice for a wedding that everyone proceeds to dance to earnestly.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of an explicit hip-hop song at a wedding is a solid visual/auditory gag. The commitment of everyone dancing to it without noticing the content is the joke's engine. Gets a solid laugh from the incongruity.

jokes.text: Stu? You're avoiding me? Hey, Melissa. Oh, my god. What happened to your tooth? Have you met Alan? Tracy's brother.
jokes.setup: Melissa (Stu's controlling girlfriend) has found Stu at the wedding and confronts him.
jokes.punchline: Stu deflects her 'what happened to your tooth?' confrontation by immediately redirecting to 'Have you met Alan?' — using an introduction as an escape hatch.
jokes.explanation: Good Stu character beat — his conflict-avoidance mechanism of introducing Alan as a shield is very him. 'Have you met Alan? Tracy's brother.' is a perfect deflection because Alan is reliably awkward enough to derail any conversation.

jokes.text: I called that bed and breakfast in Napa. They said they had no record of you even checking in. That's because we didn't go to Napa. We went to Las Vegas.
jokes.setup: Stu told Melissa he was going to a Napa bed and breakfast for the bachelor party.
jokes.punchline: Stu simply states the truth — 'we went to Las Vegas' — with an exhausted matter-of-factness that suggests he's done lying.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from Stu the liar to Stu the truth-teller is well-executed — the simplicity of 'We went to Las Vegas' as a confession after elaborate deception is the joke. His exhaustion is palpable.

jokes.text: Because my best friend was getting married and that's what guys do. Really? But that's not what YOU do! Then why did I do it, huh? Because I did it! Riddle me that!
jokes.setup: Melissa is screaming at Stu for going to Vegas instead of Napa.
jokes.punchline: Stu's escalating self-defense culminates in 'Riddle me that!' — a bizarrely Batman-villain phrase deployed in a marital spat — which is both a character revelation and a genuinely funny non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: 'Riddle me that!' is an oddly perfect Stu line — he's trying to be assertive and reaching for rhetoric he doesn't quite have. The Riddler reference deployed as a logical trump card is funny because of the register mismatch.

jokes.text: Sometimes I think all you want me to do is what you want me to do. I'm sick of doing what you want me to do all the time.
jokes.setup: Stu is building toward breaking up with Melissa during the wedding reception.
jokes.punchline: His argument becomes an inadvertent tautology — 'all you want me to do is what you want me to do' — which is both technically correct and completely meaningless as a rhetorical point.
jokes.explanation: The circular logic of 'all you want is what you want' is funny as a measure of Stu's inability to construct a real argument even when he's right. The character is genuinely trying to have a spine and failing grammatically.

jokes.text: Oh, good! Because whatever this is, ain't workin' for me. Oh, really? Since when? Since you fucked that waiter on your cruise last June.
jokes.setup: Melissa is screaming 'That is not how this works!' Stu is building to a breakup.
jokes.punchline: Stu drops the bombshell — 'since you fucked that waiter on your cruise last June' — the first real Stu power move in the film. The audience has presumably been waiting for this.
jokes.explanation: Major comedic payoff. The whole film has been building Stu's subjugation under Melissa — this is his liberation moment. The specificity ('that waiter on your cruise last June') makes it land harder than a vague accusation. The 'BOOM' that follows (whether from Phil or the editing) is the audience's reaction externalized. High structure, high character integration, very quotable. This is one of the best moments in the reel.

jokes.text: You told me it was a bartender. Oh, you were right. I stand corrected. It was a bartender. You fucked a bartender.
jokes.setup: Stu has just accused Melissa of sleeping with a waiter. She corrects him — it was a bartender.
jokes.punchline: Melissa's correction of the job title of the man she cheated with is so self-incriminating that Stu can only respond 'You fucked a bartender' — the distinction somehow making it worse.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. Melissa corrects the job title of her affair partner — an act of inadvertent self-destruction. The fact that she's more bothered by the inaccuracy than the accusation tells us everything about her character. 'You fucked a bartender' as the final indictment is devastating and funny simultaneously. The specificity, the structural perfection, and the character revelation all converge. This is close to anchor-level (8.0) comedy writing.

jokes.text: You're an idiot. You're a... You... You're such a bad person. Like, all the way through to your core.
jokes.setup: Stu has just said 'You fucked a bartender.' Melissa tries to respond with an insult.
jokes.punchline: Melissa's attempt to come back with 'You're a...' — she can't even form a coherent insult. She lands on 'you're such a bad person, like, all the way through to your core' — a complete overreach that makes her look worse.
jokes.explanation: The trailing-off insult ('You're a... You...') followed by the melodramatic overreach ('all the way through to your core') is a great character exposure beat — Melissa is revealed as someone who can't mount a real defense. 'Like, all the way through to your core' is an absurdly dramatic thing to say to a dentist at a wedding.

jokes.text: Alan, shall we dance? Let's do this.
jokes.setup: Stu has just publicly destroyed Melissa. Rather than continue the argument, he pivots.
jokes.punchline: Stu turns to Alan with 'Alan, shall we dance?' — a moment of pure triumphant absurdity. Alan's immediate 'Let's do this' suggests he's been waiting for this his whole life.
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper to the Melissa confrontation. 'Alan, shall we dance?' is a formal, almost Victorian pivot from a brutal argument — the register shift is the joke. Alan's instant enthusiastic 'Let's do this' is the ideal response. This is the comedic payoff of their entire dynamic in the film.

jokes.text: Hey! I'm gonna leave forever. I'm gonna learn how to fly high.
jokes.setup: Melissa has been publicly humiliated and is leaving.
jokes.punchline: Her departing declaration — 'I'm gonna leave forever. I'm gonna learn how to fly high.' — is an unintentionally grandiose manifesto from someone who just had the worst of an argument.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh beat — Melissa's exit speeches ('I'm gonna learn how to fly high') are overdramatic and self-aggrandizing in a funny way. Functions as a coda to her character but not a crafted joke.

jokes.text: It was a real pleasure meeting you. Fuck off. I'm thinking about getting my bartender's license. Suck my dick. No, thank you.
jokes.setup: Melissa is storming out. Stu keeps engaging, escalating the callback to the bartender.
jokes.punchline: Stu's 'I'm thinking about getting my bartender's license' — taunting her with the affair — and his prim 'No, thank you' to her 'Suck my dick' is a perfect character coda.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm thinking about getting my bartender's license' as a parting taunt is brilliant — Stu rubbing in the affair by aspiring to the job title. 'No, thank you' to 'suck my dick' is the perfect Stu response: even in total victory, he maintains polite dental office decorum. Very high character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Remember, remember, remember, remember my name, babe!
jokes.setup: Melissa is making her final exit from the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Her departing line — 'Remember my name, babe!' — is an unintentional irony given that everyone in the audience has been told she cheated on Stu and nobody wants to remember her.
jokes.explanation: Mild coda to Melissa's character. Her defiant 'remember my name' as a parting shot after being completely destroyed is an ironic beat — she's framing her humiliation as a moment of power. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: I'll give it 6 months.
jokes.setup: Dougie has just said 'I gotta tell you, man, that was a gorgeous wedding.' Phil responds.
jokes.punchline: Phil's flat '6 months' prediction for the marriage — delivered at the reception, immediately after the ceremony — is a perfectly cynical anti-toast.
jokes.explanation: 'I'll give it 6 months' is Phil in one line — he just helped save the wedding at enormous personal cost and his private verdict is devastating. The economy is near-perfect (four words). Highly quotable as a marriage/life sentiment. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I just wish we could actually remember some of it.
jokes.setup: Doug says he guesses he should thank them for the bachelor party.
jokes.punchline: The acknowledgment that none of them actually remember the best-ever bachelor party is the final irony of the film's premise.
jokes.explanation: Thematic callback to the film's central irony — an epic bachelor party that nobody can remember. Functional closer to the main narrative joke. Not especially crafted but lands emotionally.

jokes.text: Hey guys. Look what I found. Whoa, that's my camera. Yeah, it was lodged in the back seat of the car. Are there photos on it? Yeah. Some of it is even worse than we thought.
jokes.setup: Everyone thinks the story is over — the wedding happened, Melissa is gone, chips are in hand.
jokes.punchline: Alan produces a camera from the car — implying photographic evidence of everything they can't remember — and 'some of it is even worse than we thought' is the perfect tease for what follows.
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation setup for the film's famous credits sequence. 'Some of it is even worse than we thought' is a great tease — after everything we've seen (tiger, baby, missing tooth, wrong Doug, lost $80k), the promise of worse is both funny and exciting.

jokes.text: We look at these pictures together, okay? One time. And then we delete the evidences.
jokes.setup: Everyone is debating whether to look at the photos or delete them immediately.
jokes.punchline: 'Delete the evidences' — Phil's slightly broken English on 'evidences' (not a standard English word) is probably intentional (the gravity of treating their night as a crime scene) and the word itself is funnier than 'evidence.'
jokes.explanation: 'Delete the evidences' is a funny, almost contractual formality — the word 'evidences' makes their night sound like a legal proceeding. The 'one time' viewing rule is also funny as an arbitrary mitigation. Good economy and quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, dear Lord! [group sees first photo from the camera]
jokes.setup: The group has agreed to look at the camera photos once before deleting them.
jokes.punchline: The first photo is apparently so horrific that someone immediately cries out 'Oh, dear Lord!' — setting up the closing credits photo montage of their lost night.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the reel. 'Oh, dear Lord!' after the buildup of 'some of it is even worse than we thought' is a great escalation cap. Functions as a launch pad for the credits sequence (not scored separately as it's outside the reel), but as a closing beat it's very effective.
